The book starts with the Norman Conquest, in the sweep its title claims, and follows the realm's politics from records, in a style meant for wide reading. Readers get early twentieth-century history writing, learned and narrative at once. It suits those tracing England's political tale in a series built to serve a new age.
8648-war-poetry-of-the-south:
William Gilmore Simms edited this 1866 anthology of Southern Civil War poetry, published by Richardson and Company the year after the war ended. The poems speak for the Confederate cause, its soldiers, its losses, and its home front, and Simms dedicates the volume to the women of the South. He frames them as having lost a cause but shown a spirit worth recording.

Battle pieces, laments, and songs of endurance sit side by side, giving a chorus of wartime feeling rather than a single poet's view. Historians value the book as evidence of how the South first told its own war story in verse. Readers should approach it as a partisan document of its time, useful for understanding Southern memory, and for hearing the war's poetry beyond the Northern anthologies.
8747-wordsworth:
F. W. H. Myers writes this life of William Wordsworth, opening with verses about a gift won from worlds not quickened by the sun. An intermingling of heaven's pomp spread on ground British shepherds tread. Chapters follow birth and education at Cambridge, residence in London and in France, Miss Wordsworth and the Lyrical Ballads, and settlement at Grasmere. The English Lakes, marriage, society, a Highland tour, Sir George Beaumont, and the death of John Wordsworth follow.

Later chapters cover the Happy Warrior and patriotic poems, children and life at Rydal Mount with The Excursion, poetic diction, Laodamia, the evening ode. Natural religion, closing with an Italian tour and ecclesiastical sonnets. Myers, a sympathetic Victorian critic, traces how a revolutionary youth became the sage of the Lakes. The life remains a graceful short biography, ideal for readers meeting Wordsworth beyond the famous daffodils.
8872-report-on-the-condition-of-the-sout:
Carl Schurz reports on the condition of the South in this 1865 Senate document, first published as Senate Executive Document number two of the thirty-ninth Congress. President Johnson transmits it in compliance with a Senate resolution of December 12, sending information on the states lately in rebellion. Schurz's report on South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana, and a report by Lieutenant General Grant on the same subject. It was read and ordered printed on December 19, 1865.

Schurz, a German-American general and reformer sent south by Johnson, travelled the defeated states and found white resistance to emancipation, Black Codes, and violence, contradicting rosier accounts. His frank findings helped shape Radical Reconstruction debates. Historians treat the report as a landmark primary source on the first months after Appomattox. Readers get a clear, unsparing view of a South deciding, painfully, what freedom would mean.
8881-a-fleece-of-gold-five-lessons-from-:
Charles Stewart Given draws five lessons from the fable of Jason and the Golden Fleece in this 1905 book, second edition revised, dedicated to his sons Kingsley and Gordon. An epigraph shows Jason and his men seizing the favourable moment of the rebound, plying oars with vigour, and passing through in safety. Contents list, among others, the ruling element and the ethics of activity, with Given's own name attached to the lessons.

The first lesson asks what constitutes a state, answering that it is not high battlements, thick walls, moated gates, proud cities, broad ports, or starred courts where low-browed baseness wafts perfume. Given turns the old myth into moral instruction for young men: courage, timing, teamwork, and character over display. Readers interested in Edwardian self-help and classical moralizing will find a short, earnest book, plain in style and confident in its classical examples.
8928-simo-n-boli-var-the-liberator-patri:
Guillermo A. Sherwell, a Mexican scholar and former rector of the National University of Mexico, wrote this life of Simón Bolívar, first printed in Washington in 1921. Bolívar, called the Liberator, led the wars that freed much of Spanish South America in the early 1800s, and is named father of five nations.

Sherwell traces Bolívar's youth, his campaigns, his statesmanship, and his sad last years, when the vast lands he freed split apart. The sketch is short and clear, meant for readers new to the hero. It still serves as a plain guide to a man whose name marks streets and states across a continent.
9568-the-frost-spirit-and-other-poems-pa:
Part one of volume two of Whittier's works opens his Poems of Nature, with The Frost Spirit at the head. The Frost Spirit, The Merrimac, Hampton Beach, and A Dream of Summer follow in a chain of New England scenes. Whittier, a Quaker poet, finds moral calm in woods, shores, and seasons. This part leads the nature group of his collected verse.

The opening run favors short lyrics over long tales, each tied to a place or a season. Frost, river, beach, and summer dream all serve as signs of a larger order. A reader gets Whittier at his most lyrical, with nature verse that is plain, devout, and easy to carry in mind.
9915-an-appeal-to-the-christian-women-of:
Angelina Emily Grimké, a South Carolina woman who had left the South, addressed this appeal to the Christian women of her home region in the 1830s. She calls on them to speak against slavery, quoting Esther's resolve to go before the king even if she perished.

Grimké argues that silence makes slaveholding women share in the sin, and that faith demands action rather than quiet disapproval. Her pamphlet became a landmark of abolitionist writing by a southern woman. Readers meet an urgent, Bible-grounded argument that helped move antislavery feeling in the North.
9941-biography-of-a-slave-being-the-expe:
Charles Thompson, a preacher of the United Brethren Church, published this account of his life as a slave in the South in 1875. He writes plainly that he is no book-maker and claims only truthfulness and honesty of purpose, hoping to do good to his own race and to all who read.

Thompson was born a slave in Atala County, Mississippi, near Kosciusko, and his story includes parting from his mother, a grief he mourns before their final separation. Later chapters follow his path to preaching and freedom. Readers get a rare firsthand slave narrative, told in a preacher's direct voice.
a-journey-into-the-interior-of-the-earth:
Jules Verne sends Professor Lidenbrock, his nephew Axel, and the guide Hans down into the earth, in Frederick Amadeus Malleson's translation, published by Ward, Lock in 1877 as the editor's note explains. The contents open with the professor and his family and a runic manuscript that poses a mystery to be solved at any price. The old document names an Icelandic crater as the door.

Forty-five chapters descend Sneffels, lose and find water, cross a vast underground sea by raft, and meet the remains of prehistoric life. Thalatta, thalatta, Axel cries at the shore. Verne mixes geology lessons with peril at every stage, and the return, through a volcanic eruption, is as wild as the descent.
apollonius-conic-sections-heath:
Thomas L. Heath published his edition of Apollonius's Conic Sections in 1896. Apollonius of Perga, called the Great Geometer, worked around 200 BCE. His Conics became the definitive ancient work on its subject.

Slice a cone at different angles and the curves appear. Circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas all arise from that single cut. Apollonius worked out their properties in propositions of great difficulty. His names for the curves still serve mathematics today. Kepler's astronomy and Newton's physics later depended on this theory. Heath's translation made the peak of ancient geometry readable in English. Few ancient scientific works waited so long for their full vindication.
beltane-the-smith: Beltane the Smith, Jeffery Farnol's medieval romance. The smith's tale unfolds. This book preserves that adventure. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. History keeps its place secure. The library keeps the document safe.
bennett-deacon-skidmore-s-letters-writte: Deacon Skidmore's letters, written for the columns of The Truth Seeker, by Bennett. The deacon's letters. This book preserves that collection. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
bradford-plymouth:
William Bradford, governor of Plymouth Colony for most of his life, wrote his history of the plantation between 1630 and 1650. The manuscript stayed in family hands, vanished during the Revolution, and resurfaced in England. It is America's founding memoir.

Bradford tells how the Separatists fled England for Holland, then crossed on the Mayflower in 1620. He describes the first winter's deaths, the treaty with Massasoit, and the colony's slow growth. His plain style carries deep faith and quiet grief. The famous line about one small candle lighting a thousand comes from these pages. The manuscript's return to Massachusetts in 1897 was greeted as a homecoming.
camilla-picture-of-youth: Camilla, picture of youth, by Fanny Burney. The young heroine. This book preserves that novel. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
captain-john-smith:
Charles Dudley Warner wrote this life of Captain John Smith for a series on American notables, and his preface states the problem plainly. Earlier biographies merely paraphrased Smith's own narrative and accepted his estimate of himself. New evidence and twenty years of critical research had cut the romance down, and Warner set out to give the connected truth in popular form.

He read everything attributed to Smith's pen and checked it against other contemporary accounts. The Pocahontas legend gets its own careful tracing across the chapters. For Smith's early adventures there is no authority but Smith, and Warner says so. The result is a demystifying portrait: a real founder of Virginia, smaller than his legend and more interesting for it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-arbr: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Arbroath describes a Benedictine monastery founded on Scotland's east coast in 1178 by William the Lion and colonised from Kelso. It honoured St. Thomas of Canterbury, martyred eight years before, with whom William had been friendly. William was buried in 1214 in the eastern part of the noble church, finished in 1233. The richly endowed house built a harbour and set a bell on Inchcape Rock to warn mariners. After the Reformation its revenues passed to the Hamiltons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adam-of-murim:
Adam of Murimuth was a mid-fourteenth-century English chronicler. As a canon of St. Paul's, London, he took an active part in church and state affairs under Edward II and Edward III. His own-times history bears the title Chronicon, deeds of his time in which he himself took part. It interweaves Roman and French affairs with English, and covers 1302 to 1343 in Cottonian manuscripts.

Adam remains a principal witness for events up to 1346, after which an unknown continuator carries the narrative to 1380. His statements rest for the most part on good authority or personal observation. The impression he leaves is of an honest and truthful chronicler, though one possessed of no descriptive literary power. The entry cites Stubbs and Gross, with Gardiner and Mullinger's praise for his reliability.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adelard-of-ba:
Adelard of Bath was a twelfth-century scholastic philosopher born about 1100. He was probably English by birth and seems to have learned at Tours and Laon. He probably taught at Laon and at Paris, among the first medieval scholars seeking knowledge through travel in Greece and Asia Minor.

Those journeys apparently brought him into contact with Arabian learning. He used it especially on physical and physiological problems. He translated Euclid's geometry from Arabic and wrote two original treatises, De eodem et diverso and Quaestiones naturales. A pronounced Platonist in psychology and metaphysics, he opposed Platonic realism on universals, siding with Walter of Mortagne and the Indifferentists. His attempt to localize mental functions, under Galen and Arabian influence, is his most noteworthy psychological contribution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aelnoth:
Aelnoth was a monk and biographer known only through his 1109 Life of St. Canute the Martyr. In that work he calls himself a priest, a Canterbury native, and says Denmark has been his home for twenty-four years. That reckoning puts his departure from England in 1085.

In 1085 Denmark received certain relics of St. Alban, and it has been conjectured that Aelnoth accompanied them. In his work's title he is described as a monk, probably of Odense's Benedictine monastery of St. Canute. No record of his death survives. Huitfeld first printed his Life in 1602, Meursius reprinted it in 1746, and the Bollandists best edited it in the Acta Sanctorum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aldfrith:
Aldfrith was a Northumbrian king, son of King Oswin, who died on 14 December 705 after succeeding his brother Ecgfrith. William of Malmesbury says he was educated in Ireland, where he spent his early life and gained a love of learning and of learned men. He was versed in the Scriptures. His taste for books shows in his gift of a large piece of land in payment for a copy of the Cosmographia.

Adamnan of Iona presented him with On Holy Places in honour of his learning, and Aldhelm dedicated his metrical work to him. Aldfrith brought Northumbria back to peace and prosperity, then recalled St. Wilfrid to Hexham and later to York, then quarrelled with him over Roman and Irish schools of learning and church rule. On his deathbed he urged his successor to make peace with Wilfrid, though Bede dates the kingdom's church decline from his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anathoth:
Anathoth may take its name from Anath, a feminine Chaldean deity worshipped in Canaan. The town itself is identified with Anata, about two and a half miles north-east of Jerusalem. From its height of 2235 feet it commands a fine though desolate view toward the Dead Sea and the lower Jordan.

It ranked among the Levitical cities of Benjamin. Abiezer, one of David's valiant men, came from here, as did Jehu, an early follower of David. Abiathar the priest held lands here, to which Solomon banished him. One hundred and twenty-eight men of Anathoth returned from Babylonian exile. The name also belongs to a son of Bechor in the genealogy of Benjamin and to a signer of the covenant in Nehemiah.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-articles-of-f:
Articles of faith, from Greek arthron and Latin articulus, a joint, are certain revealed supernatural truths such as those held in the symbol, or creed, of the apostles. The terms were not employed by the fathers or by church writers in the early Middle Ages. Bernard and Richard of St. Victor used them, Richard applying them to truths having God as object and stated so explicitly as to compel assent.

Thomas Aquinas defines an article of faith as any revealed supernatural truth distinct from others yet joining them into the whole of Christian teaching. Thus creed articles announce truths distinct from each other but parts of a complete summary of truths revealed to help us gain our last end. They stand to theology as fundamental principles stand to a science, though not every revealed truth counts as an article, and theologians disagree on what makes one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aseneth:
Aseneth was the daughter of Putiphare, or Poti-phera, priest of On, whom Egypt's pharaoh gave in marriage to the Hebrew patriarch Joseph, bearing him two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. In ancient Egyptian order priests ranked second in honour only to pharaoh, so Joseph's pharaoh gave him one of the land's first princesses as wife. All Egyptologists agree, the article says, that her name contains the goddess Neith, tutelary deity of Sais.

Neith was seen as an emanation of Ammon, joined with him as the female principle in creation, her hieroglyph a shuttle, and Greeks identified her with Athene. Some read Asenath as dwelling of Neith, others as servant of Neith or dedicated to Neith. The name itself has not been found on Egyptian monuments, though similar names such as As-Ptah and As-Hathor occur, and apocryphal writings later embroidered her story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beroth:
Beroth, also called Beeroth, a city of Canaan, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. It belonged to a league of cities under Gibeon whose land the Israelites under Joshua invaded. To escape destruction, its people came to Joshua disguised as travellers from afar and begged mercy.

Israel made a league with them, then, on finding the trick, set them to hewing wood and drawing water. The city later passed to the tribe of Benjamin, though it seems to have stayed Canaanite until the monarchy. The entry is a compact note on a Bible town remembered for a clever ruse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-judit:
The Book of Judith tells how a widow saved Bethulia from the Assyrian general Holofernes. Nabuchodonosor of Nineveh sends Holofernes against the Jews, who besiege Bethulia on the edge of the Esdrelon plain. Achior the Ammonite defends the Jews and is handed to the besieged city. Famine breaks the citizens' courage, but Judith rebukes them, enters the Assyrian camp, charms the general, and beheads him drunk, returning with his head as trophy.

A Jewish sally then routs the Assyrians, and Judith closes the book with a hymn of victory. The text survives in distinct Greek and Latin versions, the Greek holding at least eighty-four verses more. Jerome says he rendered it from Chaldaic in one night, sense for sense, from codices that differed widely. Two Hebrew versions exist, one near the Greek and one wholly different, and Greek and Vulgate dates and names sometimes disagree.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-ruth:
The Book of Ruth, a proto-canonical Old Testament writing, tells a short tale of loyalty that ends in David's line. In the days of the judges, famine drives Elimelech, Noemi, and their two sons from Bethlehem to Moab. The sons marry Moabite wives and die childless, and Noemi turns home. Ruth alone follows her, gleans barley in the field of Booz, and, as near kinsman, claims marriage through him.

After a nearer kinsman renounces his right, Booz marries Ruth, and she bears Obed, David's grandfather. A brief genealogy then links David through Booz to Phares, son of Juda. In canon, the book sits after Judges in the Septuagint, Vulgate, and English versions, but among the Hagiographa in the Hebrew Bible, which Jewish tradition attests as the older place. Its opening line, set when the judges ruled, explains its move beside Judges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-corinth:
Sophrone Pétridès's entry covers Corinth, Corinthus, a titular archiepiscopal see of Greece. Its origin belongs to prehistoric legend. About 1100 B.C. the Dorian invasion delivered the city from the Argives, making it the centre of Heracleid rule in Peloponnesus. It then waged successful wars against neighbouring cities, including Athens. A little later, under the Bacchiadae tyranny from 750 to 657 B.C., Corinth founded many colonies, among them Corcyra and Syracuse.

About 657 B.C. a revolution replaced tyranny with government based on popular election. From then Corinth took no great part in Greek history, except as the Isthmian games' scene and through the transit duty on all goods passing by its citadel. Its name scarcely appears during the Medic wars. After beginning the Peloponnesian war from 432 to 404, Corinth handed its direction to Sparta, later abandoning its alliance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dance-of-deat:
A cultural entry traces the Dance of Death, in French Danse Macabre and German Totentanz, from a fourteenth-century play to a lasting artistic theme. Born amid plague, above all the Black Death, it showed Death not as destroyer but as God's messenger summoning all ranks beyond the grave. At first Death and victims moved slowly and with dignity.

Later Death took the manner of fiddlers and musicians, and the dance was born. Plays opened with a monk's sermon on death's certainty in the churchyard, then skeletal figures emerged from the charnel house and invited victims, pope and emperor first, to follow. The entry follows the theme through wall paintings, books, and Holbein's engravings to Rethel's 1848 dance, where Death appears as hero of the Red Republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diemoth:
Diemoth lived as a devout recluse enclosed beside the church of Wessobrunn in Upper Bavaria. Her name comes from an old German word meaning humility. She was born about 1060 into a noble family of Bavaria or Swabia. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how she entered the Benedictine nunnery joined to Wessobrunn. After a long and severe probation, she won leave to live shut in a cell beside the church.

There she spent the rest of her life in prayer and in copying valuable books. Her hand was so fair that she was styled the beautiful scribe, and she copied about forty-five volumes. She died on 30 March, probably in 1130, leaving a legacy of quiet labor that later scholars still cite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-duluth:
Duluth is a diocese set up on 3 October 1889, answering to the Archdiocese of Saint Paul. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry maps it across northern Minnesota counties from Aitkin to Saint Louis, nearly forty thousand square miles. The first white men and first Catholics there were French fur traders under Groseilliers, shipping furs from the region in 1660. Daniel Greysolon Du Lhut, for whom the see city is named, came in 1679.

After years as trading post and frontier settlement, Duluth became a town in May 1857. The first priest in Minnesota and the memoirs of Ravoux and Thebaud trace the Church's growth there. The entry draws on diocesan archives and the Catholic Directory to complete the portrait of a northern see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-meredi:
Edward Meredith was an English Catholic controversialist born in 1648, whose death year is not known, though his will is dated 1715. Son of the rector of Landulph in Cornwall, he won a scholarship to Christ Church, Oxford, in 1665. In 1668 he went to Spain as secretary to Ambassador Godolphin and there turned Catholic. Back in England he debated Stillingfleet in 1671, with help from Edmund Coleman.

In 1682 he answered Samuel Johnson's attack on the Duke of York, and in 1684 he entered the Jesuit novitiate at Watten in Flanders under the name Langford. After the fall of James II he withdrew to Saint-Germain, and he lived at Rome in 1700 and 1701. He also put a Latin book of daily meditations into English as A Journal of Meditations for Every Day of the Year in 1687.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elizabeth:
Elizabeth was the wife of Zachary and the mother of John the Baptist, and this short entry gathers what the Gospels say of her. Her name means God is an oath. She came from the daughters of Aaron, and she was a kinswoman of Mary, though their exact tie is unknown. With Zachary she was just before God, walking in all the Lord's commandments without blame.

Long childless, she was promised a son in old age by the angel Gabriel. Five months later Mary visited her, and Elizabeth, enlightened from on high, greeted her cousin as the mother of my Lord. Some modern critics would even give Elizabeth the Magnificat canticle. After John's birth and circumcision the Gospels say no more of her. Greeks keep her feast on 8 September, and the Latin Church on 5 November.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faith:
Faith, in this article, means trust in God and assent to revealed truth. The Old Testament stresses steadfast trust in God's promises and covenant. The New Testament adds belief in Christ as Saviour and Lord. Faith thus joins personal trust with acceptance of what God reveals.

The article separates objective faith, the truths believed, from subjective faith, the act of believing. It also sets out two orders of knowledge, reason and revelation. Reason can know some truths about God on its own. Revelation adds truths reason alone could not reach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-blyth:
Francis Blyth, born about 1705 and dead in London on 11 December 1772, was an English Carmelite and reviser of the Douay Bible, the English Catholic translation of Scripture. Born of Protestant parents, he joined the Catholic Church as a youth and entered the Carmelite novitiate at Modena in 1723 under the name Simon Stock of the Blessed Trinity. He studied at Malta and returned to England in 1730 to serve a mission in Wiltshire.

In 1741 he became assistant chaplain, and in 1756 chaplain-major, to the Portuguese embassy in London. Embassy chapels there served as recognised places of Catholic worship, and he distinguished himself by eloquent, zealous preaching. From 1742 to 1755 he was also Vicar Provincial of the English Carmelites. In London he took the name Courtney. A man of great literary attainments, he was buried at St. Pancras, where a memorial honoured him, and he indignantly denied a charge of aiding Pombal against the Jesuits.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-cha:
Frederick Charles Husenbeth spent more than fifty years as a parish priest in a Norfolk village. In that long stretch he missed only three Sundays. Born at Bristol in 1796, he was the son of a wine merchant and a Cornish mother who had become a Catholic. He trained at Sedgley Park and Oscott and was ordained in 1820. From the mid-1820s he served the Cossey mission as chaplain to the Jerningham family.

A man of learning, humor, and old-fashioned tastes, Husenbeth kept his distance from newer devotions and from religious orders. Yet he stayed a faithful pastor to his flock. In his quiet presbytery he wrote or edited forty-nine works between 1823 and 1849. Many answered Faber and Blanco White. His best-known book remains his 1862 Life of Bishop Milner, his early patron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-genesareth: Genesareth is the name Luke 5:1 gives the Lake of Tiberias, with the form Gennesar appearing in 1 Maccabees 11:67. The entry is a short cross-reference and nothing more. It offers no history, geography, or description of its own. Instead it points readers onward to the fuller article on the Lake of Tiberias, where the lake itself is treated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-geoffrey-of-m:
Geoffrey of Monmouth, bishop of Saint Asaph and chronicler, gave England its Arthur. Born at Monmouth about 1100 to Arthur, a priest, he was schooled by his uncle Uchtryd. He met Archdeacon Walter at Oxford, who set him to his great work, the History of the Kings of Britain. It appeared before 1139 and reached final form in 1147.

Twelve books tell how Brut, great-grandson of Aeneas, founded Britain, and how later kings fared, with Arthur's legend crowning the tale. Geoffrey called it history drawn from a most ancient book, but it is truly the start of English storytelling. From Layamon to Tennyson, through Malory, Shakespeare, Milton, and Wordsworth, his legends shaped national romance and a shared British origin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-good-faith:
Good faith is a phrase for the mental and moral state of honest, even if objectively unfounded, conviction. It covers the truth of a proposition or the rectitude of a course of conduct. One in this state, so far as violating positive law or even natural law goes, is said to labor under invincible error and hence to be guiltless. A Catholic Encyclopedia article applies the idea to those outside the visible Church and to human engagements.

It is often invoked for those outside the visible affiliation of the Catholic Church. It settles degrees of right and obligation in contracts and other engagements. In prescription it is indispensable, whether for acquiring dominion or freeing oneself from a burden, and it matters for one who holds another's property. Even a person in mortal sin who comes to Communion in good faith, many theologians hold, would receive sanctifying grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haggith:
Haggith, whose Hebrew name means festive, was one of King David's wives and the mother of his fourth son, Adonias, born at Hebron before David ruled all Israel. Scripture never names her father, and the entry notes that biblical writers habitually call Adonias the son of Haggith, as if she were a woman of some mark.

Yet nothing ties her to her son's two bids for power. One was his attempt to seize the crown in 1 Kings 1, the other his fatal request for David's concubine Abisag in 1 Kings 2. Harem intrigue shaped much eastern politics, the entry observes, but no evidence places Haggith behind either move, and her brief record ends with motherhood rather than conspiracy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harold-blueto:
Denmark's King Harold Bluetooth, son of Gorm the Old, ruled a kingdom where his father served Wotan and his mother Thyra planted the first seeds of Christian faith. Defeat by Henry I in 934 forced Gorm to restore ruined churches and tolerate Christians. Harold inherited a land where Bishop Unni of Bremen preached in Jutland without yet winning the young king's baptism.

Harold strengthened the Danewerk ramparts, aided Normandy, and subdued Norway for a time. Otto the Great's demand that he accept imperial lordship over the Danish church drove him to war and, after defeat in 972, to baptism. Sees rose at Schleswig, Ribe, Aarhus, and Odense, the Lethra grove of human sacrifice stood empty, and his son Svend's pagan-backed revolt killed him in 985 or 986.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-roth:
Augsburg Jesuit Heinrich Roth, born in 1620, was among Europe's first Sanskrit scholars and a missionary at the Mogul court. Joining the Society in 1639 and reaching Goa overland through Isfahan, he worked on Salsette and served as Portuguese interpreter. He travelled on embassy to a native prince before reaching Agra, where Shah Jahan's persecution caught him as rector.

French traveller Bernier admired his mastery of Indian religious philosophy, and in 1662 Roth returned overland through Kabul for recruits, coming back to Agra in 1664. After six years learning Sanskrit from Brahmins he compiled the first Sanskrit grammar known in Europe, published through Kircher. His reports gave Europe its first news of Kabul before his death at Agra in 1668.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-essex-e:
Henry Essex Edgeworth, known in France as the Abbé Edgeworth de Firmont, was born at Edgeworthstown, Ireland, in 1745. His Protestant family converted to Catholicism and moved to Toulouse under the penal laws. Ordained in Paris, he became confessor to Madame Elisabeth, sister of Louis XVI. In 1792, when the Archbishop of Paris fled, he was left as grand vicar with the whole diocese in his care, refusing to leave France.

Summoned to the Temple prison on 20 January 1793, Edgeworth spent the night with Louis XVI and said Mass in his apartment on the morning of the execution. He rode beside him to the scaffold, where tradition credits him with bidding the king, as a son of St. Louis, ascend to heaven, though he himself neither affirmed nor denied them. Escaping to London in 1796 and then to the exiled court at Mittau, he died in 1807 of fever caught while ministering to French prisoners.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-smith:
Journalist James Smith was born at Skolland, Shetland Isles, about 1790. He died in January 1866. He spent boyhood at Skolland, a small place belonging to his mother, a member of a Bruce branch settled in Shetland in the sixteenth century. He studied law in Edinburgh and became a solicitor to the Supreme Court there. He married a Catholic lady, cousin of Bishop Macdonell of the Glengarry clan. That marriage led to his own conversion to Catholicism.

Naturally hampered in his career by his Catholic profession at that period, he turned to literature. He became the pioneer of Catholic journalism in Scotland. In 1832 he founded and edited the Edinburgh Catholic Magazine. It appeared somewhat intermittently in Scotland until April 1838. At that date Smith moved to London, and Edinburgh was dropped from the magazine's title. Publication continued from London thereafter. The entry presents a lawyer turned pioneer Catholic journalist.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-waterwo:
James Waterworth was born at St Helen's, Lancashire, in 1806. He died at Old Hall, Newark, on 28 March 1876. Educated at Stonyhurst, he went to Montrouge to enter the Jesuit novitiate, in which he did not long continue. Bishop Milner sent him to Rome's English College to study for priesthood. There he studied theology, especially patrology, working sixteen hours a day. At course's end he was recalled to Oscott, where he was ordained.

At Oscott he taught theology from 1830 to 1833, then went to assist Reverend J. Yver at Newark, where he spent over forty years as a missionary priest, taking sole charge of the mission within a year or two. In 1834 he published a pamphlet defending Berington and Kirk's Faith of Catholics against an Anglican critic named Pope. Twelve years later he published a greatly enlarged work on the same theme. The entry presents a mission priest and patristic scholar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-emanue:
Johann Emanuel Veith, a Viennese preacher born of Jewish parents at Kuttenplan in 1787 and dead at Vienna in 1876. He studied philosophy at Prague and medicine at Vienna, taking his medical degree in 1808. He soon led the veterinary school as professor and director, wrote poetry and a staged play, and published a two-volume veterinary surgery compendium.

Becoming Christian in 1816, Veith studied theology, befriended Father Hofbauer as his physician, and at Hofbauer's urging turned to preaching after ordination in August 1821. Joining the Redemptorists at Maria Stiegen, he preached there to 1830, at Saint Stephen's cathedral to 1845. Then as retired cathedral preacher until blindness in 1863, closing as a writer of devotional works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-macrory-:
John Macrory Magrath was the fifteenth-century chief historian to the O'Briens of Thomond. Born in Munster, he belonged to a family of hereditary historians, kin to the later Protestant Archbishop Miler Magrath. His fame rests on a single work, the Cathreim Thoirdhealbhaigh, the wars of Thomond.

Written in Irish and translated by S. H. O'Grady, it histories Thomond's wars from 1194 to 1318 and is of great value for the period. Magrath treats the Anglo-Normans, above all the de Clares, and the Dalcassians' efforts to repel them. He covers the internal strife of Thomond and the failed alliance of O'Brien and O'Neill, broken when neither would serve under the other. That failure led to defeat at Downpatrick in 1259 and final victory over the de Clares at Dysert O'Dea in 1318. More than a chronicle, it weighs motives, describes battles, and judges men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-johann-g:
Karl Johann Greith was a Swiss bishop and church historian, born at Rapperswyl and dead at St. Gall in 1882. He studied at St. Gall, Lucerne, and Munich, under Joseph von Görres's protection. In Paris in 1829, studying library work, he decided for the priesthood and was ordained in 1831. He became sub-librarian of St. Gall and seminary professor, defending the Church until deprived of his offices.

Sent to Rome at the English Government's instance, he gathered documents on English history from Roman libraries and archives. Back in St. Gall he became cathedral dean in 1847, took a philosophy chair in 1853, and became bishop in 1862. At the Vatican Council he opposed defining papal infallibility, yet accepted the decision loyally and pressed Döllinger to do the same. As an orator he was called the Bossuet of Switzerland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-labyrinth:
A labyrinth is a tangle of paths and passages, often underground, wound so intricately that escape grows hard. The word comes from the famed ancient or mythical mazes of Crete and Egypt.

Church pavements carried the idea in coloured marble figures called labyrinthes de pave. The finest survivor lies in the nave of Chartres, where a walker covers nearly 800 feet of windings to reach the centre, though the figure spans only thirteen yards. Paris, Reims, and Amiens once held their own, and Amiens kept its octagonal centre stone in the city museum. The figures likely hinted at the Holy City, with prayers said along the walk. Modern mazes use tall garden hedges, as at Hampton Court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-land-of-genez:
The Land of Genezareth, named in Mark 6, is a district of Palestine on the Sea of Galilee, called the country of Genesar in Matthew's parallel passage. Scholars dispute the name's origin and whether land or lake took it first.

Jerome's traditional sense, Garden of the Princes, yields to modern derivations from Hebrew kinnereth, a harp, for the lake's supposed shape, or from the fortified town Ceneroth in Nephtali. Gospel narrative and Josephus place the district west and partly north of the lake, likely along the whole west coast to the Huleh plain and Safed hills. Within it lay Capharnaum, Corozain, Magdala, and Tiberias, now mostly ruins, where much of Christ's public ministry unfolded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leavenworth:
Leavenworth is a Kansas diocese, suffragan of St. Louis, erected 22 May 1877 over the whole state under Benedictine Louis Mary Fink as first bishop. Ten years later it split into Wichita, Concordia, and Leavenworth, and later letters of 1897 shrank Leavenworth to twenty-one eastern counties and 12,594 square miles.

Its first plains missionary was Father Juan de Padilla, martyred fifty years after Columbus's discovery. Permanent Indian missions followed with Jesuits among Potawatomies and Osages, who had begged for preachers since Marquette's day and met Franciscans in 1745. Potawatomies from Michigan and Indiana reached Kansas under Father Petit. Some had been baptized by Stephen Badin, America's first ordained priest. Bishops Kenrick in 1843 and Barron in 1845 confirmed them, and they received Potawatomie prayer books in 1845.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-meath:
Meath, the largest diocese in Ireland, serves as suffragan of Armagh and spans most of Meath, Westmeath, and King's counties, with parts of Longford, Dublin, and Cavan. In old times it held eight sees, chief among them Clonard, founded in the mid-sixth century by St. Finian, Tutor of the Saints of Erin. At the Synod of Kells in 1172, Cardinal Paparo joined these sees into one.

The united see ranked first among Armagh's suffragans, ahead even of older bishops in consecration order. Meath lay in the Pale, so many Englishmen held it, including the notorious Staples, who apostatized under Edward VI and was deposed in 1554. His successor, the Cistercian Dr. Walsh, repaired the scandal: he defied Elizabeth's threats, spent thirteen years in Dublin Castle's dungeon, and died exiled at Alcala in Spain, honoured in Irish martyrologies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missouri-test:
The Missouri Test-Oath was imposed by the constitution framed at St. Louis in January 1865. Its convention was chosen by a fraction of the voters, most men of voting age being in the Confederate or Federal armies, in guerrilla companies, or fugitives from their homes. The constitution took effect in July 1865, and no one could vote on it without first taking the test oath it provided.

A reign of terror, with arson, robbery, and murder, accompanied its enforcement. The oath barred from voting, teaching, preaching, and practising law all who had aided the Confederacy or even sympathized with it. Priests and ministers who refused it were prosecuted. The United States Supreme Court later struck down such test oaths as ex post facto laws and bills of attainder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nazareth:
Nazareth is the Galilean town where the Blessed Virgin dwelt when the Archangel announced the Incarnation, and where Christ lived until thirty, unknown and obedient to Mary and Joseph. New Testament manuscripts spell the name variously, Nazaret, Nazareth, Nazara, Nazarat and the like. In Eusebius and Saint Jerome it is Nazara, in modern Arabic en Nasirah, which seems the correct name. Its etymology is neser, a shoot, rendered flos, flower, in Isaiah 11, applied to the Saviour.

Nazareth lies in the southernmost Lebanon hills, just before they drop to the Esdraelon plain, in a hollow plateau about 1,200 feet above the Mediterranean, between hills rising to 1,610 feet. Ancient Nazareth filled a triangular hillock pointing south, bounded northwest by Jewish tombs. The entry covers its churches, the grotto of the Annunciation, pilgrimage, and the town's modern life under Franciscan care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perth:
Perth was a diocese of Western Australia, suffragan to Adelaide, stretching from the Moore River to the South Australian border. Its first Catholics were poor Irish settlers who arrived about seventy-five years before the entry, with no priest of their own. Archbishop Polding of Sydney sent Father John Brady, a Cavan man who had laboured twelve years in Mauritius, as vicar-general for the west.

Brady reached Perth in December 1843 with a Dutch ex-chaplain and a catechist, and Governor Hutt gave land for church, presbytery, and school. Ordained bishop at Rome in 1845, he returned with missionaries and six Sisters of Mercy from Carlow. The scattered flock numbered just 306 among 4,600 whites in 1848. Northern missions to Aboriginal peoples, including Father Confalonieri's work, cost lives but won hundreds of converts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plymouth:
The Diocese of Plymouth covers Dorset, once in the old Salisbury diocese, plus Devon, Cornwall, and the Scilly Isles, once the ancient Exeter diocese. After the Reformation the counties answered to three archpriests and fourteen vicars apostolic. Pius IX's Brief Universalis Ecclesiae of 29 September 1850 cut the three counties away from the Western District to form the new diocese.

George Errington of Saint John's, Salford, became its first bishop, consecrated 25 July 1851 by Cardinal Wiseman. He took possession 7 August at Saint Mary's, East Stonehouse, where he counted seventeen secular and six regular priests with twenty-three missions. He set up his cathedral chapter 26 November 1853 and gathered a synod at Ugbrooke Park in February 1854.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portsmouth:
Portsmouth diocese was created by Leo XIII's brief of 19 May 1882 from western Southwark, as set up when England's hierarchy returned in 1850. It covers Hampshire and Berkshire, the Isle of Wight, and the Channel Islands, nearly matching old Winchester's bounds. Rome avoided the old government centre and chose Portsmouth, the great naval port, as cathedral city.

John Virtue was its first bishop and organizer. He began with about seventy priests and forty missions and a partly built large church for a cathedral. His eighteen years brought slow, steady growth: new missions, religious communities, and more clergy. He enlarged the cathedral, finished its interior, built an episcopal residence and adjoining hall, and extended Woolhampton's diocesan college through a benefactress's generosity. His influence in Portsmouth was great.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preparation-f:
Spiritual writers agree that the only full preparation for death, as a rule, is a righteous life. To treat it as a set exercise with little heed to one's past life is a grave error.

First comes the call of the priest. The Roman Ritual bids the pastor hasten to a sick flock member at the first word of illness, with no wait for a summons. Extreme Unction rests on James 5:14-15. The sick man calls the church's priests, who pray over him and anoint him with oil in the Lord's name. The prayer of faith saves him, raises him, and wins pardon for his sins. It comes but once in one illness, unless a marked mending is followed by fresh danger. Failure to seek its grace from sheer sloth is a venial sin, though no precept to receive it can be proved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-of-in:
Richard of Ingworth was one of the first Franciscans to carry the order's preaching into England and beyond. He arrived with Agnellus and his friars in 1224, already a priest and well on in years. Tradition credits him as the first Franciscan to preach north of the Alps. He helped set up the first Franciscan house in London, and the early convents at Oxford and Northampton also owed much to his work.

For a while he acted as custodian in Cambridge. In 1230 he stood in as vicar of the English province while Agnellus attended a general chapter at Assisi. Later he was named provincial minister of Ireland. In 1239 he gave up that post and set out as a missionary to the Holy Land. He died on that journey, leaving behind the record of a founder whose energy shaped the order's English beginnings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-smith:
Richard Smith was a Tudor theologian whose career swung with every change of religion in England. Born in Worcestershire in 1500 and educated at Merton College, Oxford, he became registrar of the university in 1532. Henry VIII named him the first Regius Professor of Divinity in 1536. He went on to hold a string of London and Oxford posts, including the mastership of Whittington College.

Under Edward VI he lost his professorship, reportedly after yielding under pressure, and disputed publicly with Peter Martyr in 1549. Mary restored his preferments, and he took a leading part in the proceedings against Cranmer, Ridley, and Latimer. Elizabeth's accession stripped him of everything again. After a brief imprisonment he escaped to Douai, where Philip II made him dean of St Peter's. When Douai University opened in 1562, he became its chancellor and theology professor, but died within months. His many controversial works defended the Mass, clerical celibacy, and justification.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabaoth:
Sabaoth is the Hebrew plural of host or army. The word occurs almost only beside the Divine name as a majestic title for the Lord of Hosts, also given as the Lord God of Hosts. Its origins and precise meaning are matters of more or less plausible conjecture.

Some scholars hold the hosts to be, at least primitively, Israel's armies, over whom Jehovah exercised protecting influence. Others hold the word refers to heaven's hosts, the angels, and by metaphor the stars and entire universe. The latter view gains from the title's absence in the Pentateuch and Josue, though Israel's armies are often mentioned there. It is quite common in the prophetic writings, where the more exalted and universal meaning fits naturally.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbath:
The Sabbath is the seventh day of the week among the Hebrews, counted from sunset to sunset, Friday evening to Saturday evening. It was a day of rest sanctified to the Lord. All work was forbidden, including strangers as well as Israelites, beasts as well as men. Forbidden acts mentioned include cooking, gathering manna, plowing, lighting a fire, gathering wood, carrying burdens, and trading. Travelling with a religious object was not forbidden.

At a later period all movement was restricted to 2,000 cubits, a sabbath day's journey. A complete stop to work was required on just two days: the Sabbath and the Day of Atonement. Wilful violation was punished with death. The work ban made it necessary to prepare food and needs the day before, the day of preparation or Parasceve. Besides rest, special observances were prescribed: doubled daily sacrifices and new loaves of proposition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-seerth:
Seerth, a Chaldean see in the Ottoman east that appears to have succeeded the older see of Arzon, is the subject of this compact entry. Nestorian bishops of the fifth and sixth centuries are known for the district. Catholic titular bishops began under Julius III. The town itself, chief place of a district in the Bitlis province, held about 15,000 people. It had orchards, vineyards, gypsum works, and makers of arms and printed cloth.

Dominicans ran a mission there. The Catholic bishop, Addai Scher, was noted for his editions of Syriac texts. American Protestant schools also worked in the town. The diocese counted 3,000 faithful, 20 priests, 24 churches or chapels, 43 stations, and three primary schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Nazareth began in December 1812, when Father Benedict Joseph David founded a community at his seminary farm near Bardstown, Kentucky. He had found children without teachers and sick and aged neighbours without care in the surrounding missions. The first sisters lived in a log house, spun wool and flax, and wove cloth for themselves and for the seminarians. Father David named that first house Nazareth, and the name stayed with the mother-house.

The community grew from teaching and nursing work in Kentucky. Its sisters later ran schools, orphanages, and hospitals, and took the name Sisters of Nazareth to stand apart from other Sisters of Charity. Mother Seton could not spare sisters from Emmitsburg to train the new group, though Bishop Flaget had asked her to. The congregation kept its Kentucky roots while its houses spread.

The Sisters of Charity of Saint Elizabeth began at Newark, New Jersey, in 1859. Mother Mary Xavier Mehegan founded the community after twelve years with the Sisters of Charity of Saint Vincent de Paul in New York. Bishop Bayley of Newark had asked the New York superior for sisters, and the new group soon opened the first Catholic hospital in New Jersey at Saint Mary's, Newark.

On 2 July 1860 the mother-house moved to the old Chegaray mansion at Madison, vacated by Seton Hall College. An academy opened the same year and took the name Saint Elizabeth, honoring Mother Elizabeth Seton, foundress of the American Sisters of Charity. A change in head-dress followed in 1874, when a white cap with a black veil replaced the black cap Mother Seton had adopted. A normal training school for young sisters later stood at the mother-house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-st:
The Sisters of Saint Elizabeth, generally called Grey Nuns, sprang from an association of young ladies formed in 1842 at Neisse in Prussia. Dorothea Klara Wolff founded the group with Mathilde and Maria Merkert and Franziska Werner. They tended helpless sick people in their own homes, without pay, including those who could not or would not enter hospitals.

The foundresses sought to train members for hospital care and to affiliate with established confraternities, but resistance to abandoning itinerant nursing broke the attempt. The association dissolved, many new members joined the Sisters of Saint Charles Borromeo, and the foundresses left the novitiate they had entered. Klara Wolff and Mathilde Merkert died shortly after, yet the congregation later grew to 2,565 sisters with about 100 postulants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
Founded at Dublin in 1857 by Margaret Aylward, under the direction of John Gowan, the Sisters of the Holy Faith care for Catholic orphans. Pius IX called Aylward a confessor of the Faith after she spent six months in prison for saving Catholic orphans from proselytizers. The superior general lives at Glasnevin, where the sisters run a boarding school for young ladies.

At Saint Brigid's Orphanage in Dublin nearly three thousand orphans were trained and placed in trades and situations. The sisters also run primary schools, private day schools, infants' schools, and junior boys' schools. Their Coombe and Strand Street houses in Dublin feed the poor breakfast daily and give them clothing. Across fourteen Dublin convents they care for about seven thousand children, with a further community in the Diocese of Ossory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sloth:
Sloth, one of the seven capital sins, generally means disinclination to labour or exertion. Thomas Aquinas calls it sadness in the face of a spiritual good one must achieve, and Rickaby renders its Latin name acedia as the don't-care feeling. A person sees virtue beset with difficulties and chafes under God's restraints. He finds the narrow way weary, so right living inspires disgust rather than joy because of its laboriousness.

In this common sense sloth is not a specific vice for Thomas. It is a circumstance of all vices, and ordinarily lacks mortal malice unless it drives a person to defy a serious obligation. Thomas completes the definition as torpor before spiritual good which is divine good: formal distress at what one must do for God to keep friendship with God. So understood, sloth directly opposes charity and is mortal unless advertence or full consent is lacking.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-for-t:
Founded at Lyons, France, on 3 May 1822, the Society for the Propagation of the Faith is an international association aiding Catholic missionaries with prayers and alms. Pauline Jaricot of Lyons began the idea in 1820, when her brother's letter described the poverty of the Paris Foreign Missions. She gathered members giving one cent a week, and the group soon reached a thousand, sending offerings to Asia.

Twelve clergy and laymen met at Father Inglesi's call and formally founded the society, aiming to help all missions without regard to place or nationality. It never aids Catholic countries such as France or Italy, and withdraws once a mission can support itself. Two central councils at Lyons and Paris, each of twelve clergy and laymen serving without pay, divide the yearly offerings among the missions of the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alnoth:
St. Alnoth was a hermit and martyr who died about 700, and this entry gathers the little that is known of him. He has no proper feast day of his own. Jocelyn's life of St. Werburg presents him as a pious neatherd at Weedon who bore the bailiff's ill-treatment with great patience. He later became a hermit in a very lonely spot, where two robbers eventually murdered him.

On that ground he was honoured as a martyr, and pilgrims came in some number to his tomb at Stow near Bugbrook in Northamptonshire. The entry is short because the sources are short, yet it preserves a Saxon herdsman turned hermit whose patience, rather than learning or rank, earned him sainthood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dinooth:
Dinooth founded Bangor Iscoed on the Dee, one of early Britain's great monasteries, and this entry weighs a famous house against a shadowy founder. A North British chieftain driven into Wales, he built the community with his three sons under the patronage of Cyngen, Prince of Powys, sometime between 500 and 542. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 repeats the Triads' claim of 2400 monks keeping perpetual praise, a hundred voices each hour, day and night.

Bede links Dinooth with the conference at Augustine's Oak, but the entry doubts he could have made that journey as an aged man in 602 or 603. What survives is the monastery's fame and its delegates' stand on Easter reckoning. Readers get a founder glimpsed mainly through the institution he raised.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-hyacinth:
Hyacinth, Dominican called Apostle of the North, carried the Friars Preachers from Rome to Poland's frontiers. Born in 1185 at Lanka castle, Kamin, in Silesia, he was son of Eustachius Konski of the Odrowaz house. He studied at Cracow, Prague, and Bologna, earning at the last the title of doctor of law and divinity. Returning to Poland, he held a prebend at Sandomir. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Cracow to 15 August 1257.

With his uncle Ivo, bishop of Cracow, he went to Rome, met Dominic, and received the new order's habit at Santa Sabina in 1220, among its first. After novitiate and profession he led a mission band to Poland, founding a convent at Friesach in Carinthia on the way. In Poland sermons bore much fruit, and he founded houses at Sandomir, Cracow, and Plocko on the Vistula. The entry follows a scholar turned frontier preacher.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-jarlath:
Jarlath, patron of Tuam archdiocese, prayed six hundred times a day and taught scholars from all Ireland. Born in Connacht about 445, he studied under Benen, Benignus, then founded a college at Cloonfush near Tuam. Its fame is proved by pupils Brendan of Ardfert and Colman of Cloyne. Great teacher though he was, humility sent him about 495 to learn from Enda at Arran. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to about 540, on 26 December or 11 February.

He moved to Tuam in the sixth century's second decade and ranks in Ireland's second order of saints, which requires life to 540. Aengus's Felire praises his fasting, watching, and mortification: three hundred genuflections by day and three hundred by night, plus prophecy's gift. His feast falls on 6 June, the day his relics moved to a church built beside Tuam cathedral in his honour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-south:
John Southworth, English martyr of Tyburn, kept returning to plague-stricken Westminster until the law took him for good. Born in Lancashire in 1592, of a junior branch of Samlesbury Hall's Southworths, he was ordained at Douai's English College and sent on mission on 13 October 1619. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his martyrdom at Tyburn to 28 June 1654.

Arrested and condemned in Lancashire in 1627, he was jailed at Lancaster Castle, then the Clink in London. On 11 April 1630 he and fifteen other priests were handed to France's ambassador for transport abroad. Released from Westminster's Gatehouse in 1636, he lived at Clerkenwell, visiting plague houses to convert the dying. Arrested again in 1637, freed, jailed, freed, jailed, he was finally apprehended and executed after decades of returns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-william-of:
William of Perth, also called William of Rochester, was murdered on pilgrimage by the foundling he had adopted. Born at Perth, he was wild in youth but in manhood gave himself wholly to God's service. A baker by trade, he set aside every tenth loaf for the poor and went to Mass daily.

One morning before light he found an abandoned child on his church's threshold, adopted him, and taught him his trade. Vowing to visit the Holy Places, he set out with the boy, called Cockermay Doucri, said to be Scots for David the Foundling. After three days at Rochester, David misled him, felled him, and cut his throat for robbery. A madwoman's garland miracle on the corpse spread his fame, and Rochester's monks enshrined him. He died about 1201.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-protus-an:
Protus and Hyacinth were martyred in the Valerian persecution of 257 to 259. This entry builds on hard evidence. The Depositio Martyrum of 354 names 11 September as their day, and places their graves in the cemetery of Basilla on the Via Salaria, later the catacomb of Hermes.

In 1845 Father Marchi found Hyacinth's grave still undisturbed in that catacomb, a small niche holding ashes and burned bone wrapped in costly cloth. Its marble slab bore the original inscription for 11 September. Damasus called the pair brothers in his epitaph. When Leo IV moved many martyrs' bones, only Protus was found, while Hyacinth's remains were placed in the Propaganda chapel in 1849.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-abbey-of-:
The Abbey of Ampleforth, in Yorkshire, England, belongs to the English Benedictine Congregation. It traces continuity with pre-Reformation Westminster through Father Sebert Buckley, its last surviving monk. The present abbey began in a house given to Father Anselm Bolton by Lady Anne Fairfax, taken over by Dr Brewer on 30 July 1802. The community had wandered from Dieulouard through Acton Burnell, Tranmere, Scholes, Vernon Hall, and Parbold Hall under Dr Marsh.

On moving to Ampleforth Lodge, Marsh stayed at Parbold and Father Appleton became first prior. Parbold soon broke up and its schoolboys moved to Ampleforth. The priory became an abbey in 1890 by the bull Diuquidem, with a flourishing college attached. The Bishop of Newport, Dr Hedley, counts among its alumni, with its present superior, Abbot Smith. The monastery, finished in 1897, holds a library of some 30,000 volumes, forty-eight monks' cells, and dependent missions served by its monks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-rule-of-f:
A standard for testing belief, Latin regula or Greek kanon, is the idea at the centre of this entry. Rule of faith means something outside faith itself that serves as its norm and measure. Since faith is divine and infallible, its rule must be divine and infallible too. Faith assents to divine truths on divine authority, so God's truthfulness in revealing himself forms the ultimate, remote rule. 

Bible and divine tradition, containing revelation, serve as proximate but inanimate rules, silent witnesses that cannot interpret themselves. A living, animate rule must therefore be found. Private judgment, the Reformed answer, and the Church's magisterium, the Catholic answer, are weighed against each other in a classic piece of apologetics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodor-grand:
Jesuit historian of the Vatican Council, Theodor Granderath, is the scholar portrayed here. Born 19 June 1839 at Giesenkirchen in the Rhine Province, he died 19 March 1902 at Valkenburg. He studied at Neuss gymnasium and Tübingen, entering the Society of Jesus at Münster on 3 April 1860. Classics, philosophy, theology, and canon law filled his studies to 1874. 

Ditton Hall in England made him canon law professor in 1874 and dogma and apologetics teacher from 1876 to 1887. Exaeten in Holland then set him to succeed Schneemann on Acta et Decreta Concilii Vaticani. Rome called him in 1893, Leo XIII opening Vatican Council archives for his history. Gregorian apologetics in 1897 and 1898 preceded retirement to Valkenburg, where two volumes of his council history took shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-kilby-:
Thomas Kilby Smith, a Union general, was born at Boston in 1820 and died at New York in 1887. His family moved to Cincinnati in his childhood, where he learned soldiering under the astronomer O. M. Mitchel and studied law with Salmon P. Chase. He later served as a post office agent, marshal for southern Ohio and deputy clerk of Hamilton County.

Joining the Union army in September 1861 as lieutenant-colonel, he fought at Shiloh, taking command of Stuart's brigade on the second day. He served in the Army of the Tennessee, became brigadier-general in August 1863, and protected Admiral Porter's fleet during the Red River Expedition. After Mobile fell he commanded southern Alabama and Florida, and was brevetted major-general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-truth:
A philosophical survey of truth as a relation holding in three ways. First, between the knower and the known, called logical truth. Second, between the knower and his outward expression of knowledge, called moral truth or veracity. Third, between a thing as it exists and its idea in the mind of God, called ontological truth.

In each case the Scholastic theory makes the relation one of correspondence, conformity or agreement, the adaequatio of St. Thomas. The entry then weighs rival accounts, from the Scholastic theory through the Hegelian and Pragmatic theories to the "New" Realist view. It tests how true ideas can correspond with realities that are mostly not mental at all.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-use-of-wealth:
Wealth here means riches in the common sense, not the technical sense of economic treatises. The entry does not survey every profitable use of money for public or private good. Its question is narrower: whether any employment of wealth is obligatory, that is, bound by a positive precept. Writers on the spiritual life often say owners hold wealth in trust, yet that does not deny true ownership.

Ownership, the entry argues, is real but not unqualified, since duties burden its use. To claim one may do as one likes with one's own invites the plain answer: what value is then left to stewardship? The discussion weighs almsgiving, justice to workers, and the limits of luxury, setting out how far Christian teaching binds the rich. A compact piece of moral theology on money and duty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-edmund-ar:
Edmund Arrowsmith was an English martyr born at Haydock in 1585 and executed at Lancaster on 23 August 1628. He is famed for the many favours, spiritual and temporal, won through his Holy Hand, still venerated at St Oswald's, Ashton, near his birthplace. His parents suffered much for their faith, and as a child he was once left shivering in his nightclothes by pursuivants who dragged his parents to Lancaster jail.

He entered Douai College in 1605, but ill health broke his studies, and he was ordained priest in 1612. Lancashire became his mission field, where he won praise for fervour, zeal, and ready wit. Seized probably in 1622, he was brought before Bridgeman, Protestant Bishop of Chester, and debated with spirit. Condemned for his priesthood, he suffered at Lancaster, and his hand remains a relic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-henry-hea:
Henry Heath was an English Franciscan and martyr, son of John Heath, christened at St John's, Peterborough, on 16 December 1599, and executed at Tyburn on 17 April 1643. He entered Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, in 1617, took his Bachelor of Arts in 1621, and became college librarian. In 1622 George Muscott received him into the church.

After a short stay at the English College in Douai, he entered St Bonaventure's convent there in 1625 as Paul of St Magdalen. Early in 1643 he at last won leave for the English mission and crossed from Dunkirk to Dover dressed as a sailor. A German gentleman paid his passage and offered more money, but in St Francis's spirit Heath refused it and walked from Dover to London, begging his way, until his arrest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-mark-bark:
Mark Barkworth, alias Lambert, was a priest and martyr born about 1572 in Lincolnshire, executed at Tyburn on 27 February 1601. Schooled at Oxford, Father George, a Flemish Jesuit, converted him to the faith at Douai in 1594. In 1596 Barkworth travelled to Rome and on to Valladolid. On his way to Spain, St Benedict is said to have appeared to him in a vision, telling him he would die a martyr in the Benedictine habit.

Taken into the English College on 16 December 1596, he took priestly ordination in 1599 and set out for the English mission with Thomas Garnet. On his way he stopped at the Benedictine Abbey of Hyrache in Navarre. There his ardent wish to join the order was granted by making him an Oblate with leave to profess at the hour of death. After escaping great peril from the heretics of La Rochelle, he reached England and suffered at Tyburn.
complete-project-gutenberg-works-of-geor:
The Complete Project Gutenberg Works of George Meredith collects his writings in a single vast file. Meredith's novels, poems, and essays appear together, from The Pilgrim's Scrip aphorisms onward. The Ordeal of Richard Feverel begins with a father's system for raising his son. Evan Harrington, Diana of the Crossways, and Beauchamp's Career follow in their turns.

Readers can pass from the early romance Farina to the late political novels without changing files. The poetry includes the long sequence of love sonnets for which many know him best. Essays and the famous study of comedy on stage and in life complete the survey. The file is a working library of a difficult, rewarding author. Its prose demands patience and repays it with wit, psychological depth, and sentences unlike anyone else's.
complete-short-works-of-george-meredith:
The Complete Short Works of George Meredith gathers his shorter fiction into one large file. Meredith, known for long novels, also wrote tales and short novels of concentrated wit. The collection opens with the story of General Ople, a retired officer house-hunting beyond London. Lady Camper, his formidable neighbour, proves no common enigma.

Other tales follow lovers, schemers, and proud women through country-house comedy. The Tale of Chloe, his admired short novel of a duke's household, shows Meredith's tender side. Stories headed simply He and She close one sequence of courtship studies. Readers short of time for the great novels can meet his style here: dense, playful prose, sharp dialogue, and heroines who outthink the men around them. The file rewards browsing tale by tale.
diophantus-arithmetica-heath:

Diophantus poses equations as clever concrete puzzles about numbers. Find two numbers with given sum and product, his problems begin. Solutions must be rational, which makes the puzzles surprisingly hard. Later mathematicians named such problems Diophantine equations in his honor. Fermat scribbled his famous last theorem in a margin of this book. Heath's edition remains the standard English doorway to Greek algebra.

W. M. Flinders Petrie's Egyptian Tales, First Series, translates stories from the papyri of the Fourth to Twelfth Dynasties. Petrie notes that the oldest fiction in the world had appeared collectively only in French, in Maspero's Contes Populaires, with scattered English renderings in Records of the Past.

facing-death: Facing Death, G, a, henty's mining tale, the pit's danger. This book preserves that boys' story. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
give-me-liberty-or-give-me-death:
Patrick Henry spoke these words on March 23, 1775, at a Virginia convention in Richmond. The hosted text is the speech as later published, worded as a plea for arming the colony. Henry answers gentlemen who hope that Britain will soften. Britain's armies and fleets, he argues, are sent for no purpose but force. Ten years of polite requests have earned only fresh chains.

The speech builds to its famous close. Henry asks whether life is worth the price of chains and slavery. He says he knows not what course others may take. But as for him, he asks for liberty or death. Weeks later, fighting began at Lexington and Concord.
god-s-answers-a-record-of-miss-annie-mac:
Clara M. S. Lowe's God's Answers records the work of Annie Macpherson at the Home of Industry in Spitalfields, London, and in Canada. Lowe traces Macpherson from her first London visits in 1861, through rescue work among matchbox-makers and destitute boys and girls, to the opening of the Home of Industry in 1869.

Later chapters follow the emigration of families and of young people to Canada, beginning with the first party of boys who sailed with Macpherson in 1870. Lowe presents each rescue and each answered prayer as evidence of God's guidance, in the warm evangelical tone of the period. Readers interested in Victorian charity, child emigration, or London's East End will find here a detailed, admiring account of a pioneering rescue mission.
gone-to-earth:
Mary Webb's Gone to Earth is a novel of the Shropshire countryside, opening in the Callow, a copse of silver birch and larch on a round hill. Small clouds hurry across a vast sky and tear on the fangs of the mountains, while spring comes tentatively through the undergrowth.

Webb writes of a wild young woman of the woods, caught between the natural world she loves and the human world that would tame her. Purple mist hints at buds, honeysuckle leaves burn green, and the seasons shape the heroine's fate as surely as any character. Readers who love lyrical rural fiction will find Gone to Earth passionate, earthy and unmistakably Webb's own country.

A Foreign Affairs article asks what really happened in the Congo at the start of the 1960s. Its subject is the CIA, the murder of Patrice Lumumba, and the rise of Mobutu Sese Seko.

Lumumba, the Congo's first prime minister, was killed in 1961, months after independence from Belgium. Mobutu then ruled the country for three decades with Western support. The article weighs the agency's role in that chain of events from declassified records and testimony. For readers of Cold War history, it is a direct route into one of the era's darkest files.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_korea_Ho:
Jimmy Carter entered office in 1977 with two Korea goals: draw down American forces there, and press South Korea on its stark human rights record. This briefing book, posted in June 2017, uses declassified records to show what happened to both plans. Resistance came from an unexpected spread of directions.

South Korean President Park Chung Hee pushed back, as expected. But Carter's own top American advisers also resisted his troop withdrawal and rights pressure. The documents record a president fighting his ally and his own government at once. That double pushback explains much about why Carter's Korea policy stalled, in his officials' own words.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-:
When the Soviet Union ended in 1991, some 3,429 Soviet nuclear warheads sat outside Russia, in newly independent states. Tom Blanton and Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, number 571, published in December 2016. It marks twenty-five years of the Nunn-Lugar program that secured those weapons.

The posting's key fact is simple: none of those warheads blew up. Cooperative threat reduction paid former adversaries to dismantle and secure nuclear material together. At a moment when such cooperation had largely stopped, the anniversary set argues from results. It preserves the record of a security policy built on partnership rather than pressure alone.

On October 16, 1964, the People's Republic of China tested a nuclear device at its Lop Nur site and joined the nuclear club. William Burr edited this briefing book, posted on the fiftieth anniversary in October 2014. It publishes declassified records on that test and the American reaction.

China's entry changed the arms race from a two-power contest into something wider. Washington had debated striking the Chinese program before it succeeded. The documents let readers follow a feared event as it arrived, in the reporting of the government that had tracked the program for years. The anniversary frame makes the set a clean starting point on China's bomb.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
In February 1946 American diplomat George Kennan sent the Long Telegram from Moscow, the cable that framed containment of the Soviet Union. Svetlana Savranskaya edited this briefing book, posted in February 2021 for its seventy-fifth anniversary. It adds a remarkable coda from 1990.

Soviet reformer Alexander Yakovlev discussed Kennan's famous X article with Kennan himself, in a Moscow meeting whose record was previously unpublished. The posting also notes that Kennan dictated the Long Telegram while laid up in bed with flu and a sinus condition. A doctrine that governed forty years began as a sick man's dictation, and ended with its author debating it in a changed Moscow.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern:
Presidents Donald Trump and Mauricio Macri issued a joint statement on April 27, 2017. The National Security Archive posted this account of what it meant for Argentina's long wait for American records. The subject is declassified diplomacy: Washington handing over files on the human rights abuses of Argentina's 1976 to 1983 dictatorship.

Releases of that kind began under earlier administrations, and the posting tracks the policy continuing across a change of party in the White House. For families of the disappeared, each new batch of files can still name names, dates, and places. Readers get a compact update on a slow, practical form of justice work, where paperwork from one country helps another country face its past.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_Cyber: In September 2018, the Justice Department unsealed a criminal complaint against Park Jin Hyok. He is a North Korean hacker tied to some of the most damaging cyber operations ever charged. They include the Sony Pictures attack and the WannaCry outbreak. A National Security Archive cyber brief, published on September 6, 2018, presents that complaint and its place in the record of North Korean cyber operations. The brief gathers the government's own allegations in one place, giving readers the formal American case against Pyongyang's hackers as prosecutors wrote it.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cyber-vault_The_c:
Section 215 of the law known as FISA let the National Security Agency collect Americans' phone records in bulk, a program revealed in 2013 and fought over ever since. A National Security Archive news post, edited by Rosemary Tropeano, reports the NSA's own verdict: the agency formally recommended ending the program, as the Wall Street Journal reported.

The headline borrows an old line about a game not being worth the candle, and the post asks the question outright: was Section 215 worth it, or even effective? When the agency that ran a surveillance program advises killing it, the debate changes ground. Readers get a compact account of a rare official admission, useful for anyone following how mass surveillance programs are justified, judged, and sometimes retired.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_guatemala_Guatema:
In 1999, the National Security Archive published Guatemala's Death Squad Dossier, a stolen logbook that recorded the kidnapping and disappearance of 183 people by government agents between 1983 and 1985. In June 2021, the Archive reported what the dossier finally made possible: police arrested eleven former military and security officials in connection with those crimes.

The posting, edited by Kate Doyle, calls the arrests the first real chance of justice for the dossier's victims, twenty-two years after the document surfaced. A logbook kept by the killers themselves is rare evidence, and its path from secret file to arrest warrant shows why preserving such records matters. Readers get the story of a document that waited decades to do its work in court.
grisly-grisell-or-the-laidly-lady-of-whi: Grisly Grisell, or The Laidly Lady of Whitburn, a tale of the Wars of the Roses, by Charlotte Yonge. The lady's tale. This book preserves that historical novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
guns-of-the-gods-a-story-of-yasmini-s-yo: Guns of the Gods, a story of Yasmini's youth by Talbot Mundy. The princess's early tale. This book preserves that adventure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
history-of-the-impeachment-of-andrew-joh:
Edmund G. Ross wrote the history of the impeachment of President Andrew Johnson from inside the event: he was the Kansas senator whose vote helped acquit. Ross lays out the collision between Johnson and the Republican Congress over Reconstruction after the Civil War. The House impeached the president in 1868 for alleged high crimes and misdemeanors, and the Senate tried him with the chief justice presiding.

Acquittal came by a single vote, and Ross argues that conviction would have wrecked the presidency itself. His preface warns new generations that the constitutional principles at stake outlive the quarrel. The book is part history, part defense brief, and still the insider account of America's first presidential impeachment trial.
increasing-human-efficiency-in-business-:
Walter Dill Scott, an American psychologist, applied his science to the office and factory floor in Increasing Human Efficiency in Business. Scott argues that tools and methods had improved beyond measure while the human worker stayed unstudied.
