His chapters take up one mental lever at a time: imitation, competition, loyalty, and concentration.

Later chapters treat wages, pleasure in work, love of the game, relaxation, and the slow rate of real improvement. Habit and judgment close the book, with practice joined to theory. Scott wrote for managers who wanted output without breaking people. The result is an early classic of industrial psychology, plain in style and full of workplace examples.
jeanne-d-arc-her-life-and-death:
Margaret Oliphant wrote Jeanne d'Arc: Her Life and Death for the Heroes of the Nations series in 1896, and inscribed it to a cousin in love of their common heroine. Oliphant begins with France in the fifteenth century, a land of war where Joan, a peasant girl of Domrémy, heard voices and rode to the Dauphin. Chapters follow the relief of Orléans in May 1429, the Loire campaign, and the coronation at Reims that July.

Defeat, capture at Compiègne, and the long trial at Rouen fill the second half, hearing by hearing, down to the abjuration and the burning in May 1431. Oliphant, a Scottish novelist of formidable output, writes warm narrative history for general readers, skeptical of legend and loyal to the girl.
keineth:
Keineth is a girls' book by Jane Abbott, dedicated to all the little girls she knows. The opening chapters show Keineth's world changing fast. The Orphan Asylum stands in her old world, and Overlook in her new one. Keineth writes to her father, and a figure named Pilot comes into the story.

Music fairies, Abbott says, were put into Keineth's fingers by the fairies of the glade. Alice runs away, and Pilot wins a home. Aunt Josephine's arrival and school days carry the story on. Bobby's triumph and the glade revisited close the contents shown. Abbott writes a warm story of a girl finding family, music, and a place to belong.
kenilworth:
Kenilworth is Walter Scott's novel of Queen Elizabeth's court, named for the castle where its climax falls. Its contents list forty-six chapters, though the sample gives their numbers without titles. The story turns on the Earl of Leicester's secret marriage to Amy Robsart. Leicester hides his wife while he courts the queen's favor at court.

Elizabeth's pride and jealousy make the secret deadly once it stirs suspicion. Scott builds to the great revels at Kenilworth Castle, staged to dazzle the queen. Amy's hidden life and Leicester's ambition collide there in tragedy. Published in 1821, the novel ranks among Scott's most famous court romances. This edition presents it plain, with the chapter list marking its long road to Kenilworth.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
John Lothrop Motley wrote this history of John of Barneveld, Holland's Advocate. The opening volume covers 1609, as the Twelve Years' Truce began. Motley treats the work as a sequel to his histories of the Netherlands. He also meant it as an introduction to the Thirty Years' War.

His preface argues the Dutch and German wars formed one long tragedy. Eighty years of struggle linked Holland's freedom with Germany's breakup. Barneveld directed Dutch councils through the uneasy pause in fighting. The volume sets his career inside the gathering European storm. The truce with Spain frames every council scene that follows in the volume.
life-of-adam-smith:
John Rae published this life of Adam Smith with Macmillan in 1895. Early chapters cover Smith's early days at Kirkcaldy, his birthplace. His father died young, and his mother raised the future economist. The burgh school and its schoolmaster's drama shape his boyhood.

Smith then studies at Glasgow under Simson and Hutcheson. Hutcheson's economic teaching and influence receive close attention. A Snell exhibition carries Smith on to Oxford and Balliol College. Rae questions Oxford's learning while noting Smith's gratitude to it. Smith's taste for mathematics showed early at Glasgow College. His early connection with David Hume also begins during those years.
light-life-and-love-selections-from-the-:
W. R. Inge selected these writings from medieval German mystics. London's second edition appeared in 1919. Contents name Eckhart first, then Tauler and Suso. Ruysbroek and the Theologia Germanica complete the gathering.

Inge argues the Imitation of Christ came late in the movement. Thomas a Kempis merely toned down Eckhart's characteristic doctrines. True strength lies a full hundred years earlier, he writes. The thirteenth-century awakening, with Francis and Dominic, frames the selections. Meditations on the Seven Words from the Cross join the contents. Bonaventura and Aquinas frame the age Inge calls chivalrous in religion.
lilith:
George MacDonald, a Scots priest and poet, wrote this dark tale for grown readers in 1895. It stands by Phantastes as one of the two peaks of his work. MacDonald wrote late in life, and the book bears the weight of his thought on death.

A man finds a gate in his house to a world of shade and strange laws. There he meets Lilith, the first wife of Adam in old lore, fair and dread at once. The dream walk through that world is a quest for rest, for the dead and the living both.
liza-of-lambeth:
W. Somerset Maugham first published this novel with Heinemann in 1897. It opens on the first Saturday afternoon in August. Broiling heat gives way to a cooler evening in Lambeth. Everyone on Vere Street has come outdoors to enjoy it.

Forty houses face forty identical houses across the street. Dingy grey brick and slate roofs repeat without variation. Children claim the cemented street for noisy cricket games. Coats serve as wickets, and rags or tennis balls fly. Bundles of rags or old tennis balls served the cricketers. Eighty houses matched one another more closely than peas, Maugham writes.
louis-agassiz-as-a-teacher-illustrative-:
Louis Agassiz as a Teacher gathers extracts that show how the great naturalist taught. Lane Cooper, a Cornell professor of English, chose the pieces and wrote the notes. A poem by Lowell opens the book, praising eyes trained to truth. Cooper says his own teaching follows Agassiz's method in essence.

The extracts let students and colleagues tell how Agassiz made them learn. His way was to set the thing itself before the student and demand close looking. Fish, fossils, and shells became teachers in his hands. The book is short but full of wisdom on real study. Teachers of any subject can profit from its pages.
lyrics-of-earth:
Lyrics of Earth is a book of nature poems by Archibald Lampman. Copeland and Day published it at Boston in 1895. Lampman was a Canadian civil servant who wrote in his spare hours. Titles here include 'The Sweetness of Life' and 'April in the Hills.'

'Forest Moods,' 'The Meadow,' and 'In May' show his true subjects. He watches snow, returning seasons, and quiet fields with a painter's eye. His verse is calm, clear, and full of Canadian light. Lampman died young, but his work lived on at home. Many call him the finest nature poet Canada has produced. These lyrics show why that praise endures.
macbeth:
Macbeth is William Shakespeare's tragedy of ambition and murder. Its scenes move from a heath near Forres to Macbeth's castle at Inverness. Three witches greet Macbeth and Banquo with strange prophecies. Lady Macbeth steels her husband to kill King Duncan in his sleep.

The crown won by murder brings no peace to either of them. A banquet is haunted by Banquo's ghost in the room of state. The witches' cauldron brews fresh riddles in a dark cave. Macduff's family is slaughtered at Fife, and revenge gathers in England. At Dunsinane a moving wood fulfills the prophecy at last. It is Shakespeare's shortest and most terrible tragedy.
manhood-perfectly-restored-prof-jean-civ:
Manhood Perfectly Restored is an advertising tract for the Civiale Remedial Agency. The agency sold from 174 Fulton Street, New York. Its remedy was Professor Jean Civiale's soluble urethral crayons. The pamphlet calls them a quick, painless, and certain cure for impotence.

Lost manhood, nervous debility, and kindred troubles fill its list. The cover was sent sealed, and only when requested. Bold type claims official recognition and hospital adoption. Such claims were the stock style of mail-order medicine sellers. The tract survives as evidence of nineteenth-century medical marketing. It shows how shame and hope were used to sell cures.
many-thoughts-of-many-minds-a-treasury-o:
Many Thoughts of Many Minds is a treasury of quotations from all lands and ages. Louis Klopsch compiled it for the Christian Herald in 1896. His preface counts nearly four hundred subjects in the small volume. Upwards of twenty-five hundred extracts fill its pages.

The passages come from standard authors of recognized ability. They are arranged by topic, to serve the largest circle of readers. Preachers, speakers, and writers mined such books for gems. A apt line could crown a sermon or a speech. Klopsch hoped his treasury would help all who received it. The book preserves what one age found worth quoting. It is a compact storehouse of received wisdom.
memoir-correspondence-and-miscellanies-f:
Thomas Jefferson Randolph edited Jefferson's papers in a four volume set. Volume two opens with a letter to Richard Henry Lee. Jefferson wrote it from London on April 22, 1786.

He sends a new lamp, bought after a fruitless search in Paris. On trade, he warns that Britain seeks no pact with America at all. No party there, in or out of power, favors such a link, he says. The letters show a envoy at work in goods, trade, and state craft. A steel plate of Jefferson, from a Stuart painting, fronts the set. Such plates mark the 1829 issue of his papers.
mike-and-psmith:
P. G. Wodehouse's school novel sends Mike Jackson to a new school, Sedleigh, in this story first copyrighted in 1909. There Mike meets Psmith, the calm, talkative boy who becomes his closest ally. Chapter titles promise guerrilla warfare, unpleasantness in the small hours, and a fire brigade meeting. A mystery grows around Jellicoe, missing evidence, and a trail of shoes.

Mr. Downing hunts the culprit like a sleuth-hound while Mike receives a secret commission. The plot clears through Adair's methods and ends with peace declared. The final chapter is the cricket match, Sedleigh against Wrykyn. Wodehouse mixes schoolboy crime, sport, and Psmith's unshakable politeness.
minnesota-its-character-and-climate-like:
Ledyard Bill published this guide to Minnesota in 1871. Bill had already written A Winter in Florida. His preface says Minnesota enjoyed a superior reputation for climate, soil, and scenery. He sets out to explain the real grounds of that pre-eminence.

The book sketches other resorts favorable to invalids besides Minnesota. Copious notes on health accompany the travel material. Bill also gives hints to tourists and emigrants planning the journey. In his day, doctors sent consumptive patients west and north for dry air, and such guides shaped where they went. Minnehaha Falls illustrates the scenery he praises.
muir-boyhood-youth:
John Muir published The Story of My Boyhood and Youth in 1913, the year before his death. It recalls his childhood in Scotland and his family's move to a Wisconsin farm in 1849. The wild boyhood, he shows, made the conservationist.

Muir describes a strict father, long farm labor, and the birds and woods he loved in secret. He taught himself math and whittling, carving clocks and clever machines before dawn. The Wisconsin wilderness, with its prairies and marshes, became his first school. Readers of his mountain books will find their roots in these farm chapters. The book ends as he leaves the farm for the wider world.
my-lady-of-the-north:
Randall Parrish calls this Civil War tale the love story of a gray jacket. A dispatch for Longstreet opens the plot. Night rides, unwelcome guests, and struggles in the dark follow. The hero falls into enemy hands more than once.

Chapters bring Sheridan, death sentences, and staff balls. A battle in the Shenandoah anchors the war scenes. Hand-to-hand fights and lost regiments raise the stakes. Parrish was a master of swift historical romance. V1 praised his color and pace. The tale pairs divided loyalties with love, told at a gallop through the war's most storied valley.
my-life-in-the-south:
Jacob Stroyer tells his own life in slavery and war in this book. A new, enlarged edition came out at Salem, Massachusetts, in 1898. John Wright Buckham praises Stroyer's keen memory in a note. He calls the tale touching, thrilling, and trustworthy.

An 1879 note calls it the inside view of slavery itself. It shows how the enslaved felt under the yoke, in their own words. Such study, the note argues, is still needed for justice. Stroyer writes in a simple, direct style. His book stands as firsthand witness, a Black man's own record of bondage, war, and freedom's hard start.
my-year-of-the-war-including-an-account-:
Frederick Palmer, an American reporter at the British front, wrote this war book. Its contents open with praise for the brave Belgian. Mons, Paris, and the chase of Von Kluck follow. Christmas in Belgium comes under German rule.

Later chapters enter winter trenches and the fight at Neuve Chapelle. Palmer rides with the guns and visits a bombing school. The last third tours the Grand Fleet at sea. He boards destroyers, the Inflexible, and the fleet flagship. Submarine hunts close the record. Palmer gives plain, close reporting on the war's first year, by land and sea.
narrative-of-the-voyage-of-h-m-s-rattles:
John MacGillivray, naturalist to the expedition, wrote this voyage account. H.M.S. Rattlesnake sailed under Captain Owen Stanley from 1846 to 1850. The Admiralty sanctioned the book, issued in two volumes in 1852. Surveys in New Guinea and the Louisiade Archipelago fill it.

An added account tells of E. B. Kennedy's Cape York expedition. MacGillivray dedicated the work to Stanley's mother, in her son's memory. Stanley died before the book appeared in print. The Rattlesnake charted reefs and coasts key to Australian trade. Its naturalist's notes on new lands, peoples, and species still serve science and history.
nasa-tm-19640000194-lunar-flight-study-s:
A Marshall Space Flight Center team wrote this volume of the Lunar Flight Study Series. Volume two studies Earth to Moon transits using star position data. The method relies on the best computer program then available. Part two treats the return flight from lunar orbit to Earth.

Catalog notes list what the part computes for the trip home. Trajectory, reentry conditions, and landing site all come under study. Launch settings from the Moon, called injection conditions, are worked out too. A crew returning from the Moon must hit Earth's air at a safe angle. Studies like this one laid the path math Apollo later flew.
nasa-tm-19640023644-some-results-of-rock: Goddard Space Flight Center issued this report in June 1964 on rocket results from the quiet D region. The D region is the lowest layer of the ionosphere, high above Earth. Catalog notes say Nike-Apache sounding rockets measured electron density profiles there on quiet, mid-latitude days. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable body text, so its measured profiles cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660006036-life-in-space-and-hu:
Su-Shu Huang reviews five books together under the heading of life in space and humanity on Earth. The books are by Shapley, who appears twice, by Merrill, by Cameron, and by Sullivan. Their subjects run from stars and galaxies to interstellar communication and the search for other minds. Shapley's two titles are named first in the contents.

Huang groups the review under the astronomer's gift to humanity. He opens with a tale of the Buddha gaining wisdom under a tree. That broad frame suits books that mix astronomy with big human questions. The review preserves how a space scientist read the popular astronomy of his day, and judged its worth for general readers.
nasa-tm-19660009018-boundary-value-probl:
Hugo L Ingram at Marshall applied optimization theory to trajectory problems in this report, and found a boundary value problem at the center. A boundary value problem fixes conditions at two ends, not one. Best-path problems for rockets naturally take that form. The resulting equations are nonlinear, and not all conditions are given at the same point, Ingram notes.

Three practical numerical methods for solving such problems are discussed. The most efficient method is then explained in detail on a sample problem. Ingram adds that the methods fit other boundary value problems too. Trajectory planning for the Saturn program gave this mathematics a direct, daily use at Marshall.
nasa-tm-19660017919-observations-of-the-:
Principal results from an experiment on the IMP-1 satellite, also called Explorer XVIII, are discussed in this Ames report. The experiment studied the solar wind and how it interacts with Earth's magnetic field. Its main aim was to measure the energy and flow traits of the positive ions in the passing plasma. A curved plate electrostatic analyzer did the measuring on board.

The satellite was launched from Cape Kennedy on November 26, 1963. Its orbit was highly stretched, reaching about thirty-one Earth radii out. That path carried the instruments through both calm and disturbed regions. Early solar wind data of this quality shaped the field's first real picture of the wind.
nasa-tm-19660024079-effect-of-target-mat:
Robert G. Thomson and E. T. Kruszewski of NASA's Langley Research Center wrote this paper for the Seventh Hypervelocity Impact Symposium, held in Tampa, Florida, in November 1964. Their subject is what happens when a very fast projectile punches through a thin metal plate. That question matters for spacecraft, which face tiny particles moving at extreme speeds.

The authors study a visco-plastic flow theory. That kind of theory treats the plate metal as a material that flows under sudden, violent stress. They test whether the theory can predict perforation and the ballistic limit of a plate. The ballistic limit is the speed below which a projectile fails to get through. Their work links that limit to the yield strength of the target material.
nasa-tm-19660024129-the-solar-wind-and-i:
Charles P. Sonett, of the Space Sciences Division at NASA's Ames Research Center in California, reviews the solar wind in this paper. The solar wind is a stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun. Sonett focuses on what happens when that stream reaches Earth's magnetic field, the magnetosphere.

He sums up the wind's known properties and discusses the bow shock formed ahead of Earth. He compares the shock's required conditions with evidence from several space probes. The paper stresses the flow behind the shock, plus particle spectra and turbulence in that region. Sonett also warns that analysis of IMP satellite data was still very early.
nasa-tm-19660030632-electrical-maintenan:
W. E. Neisler, of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, presented this talk in January 1964. His subject is unglamorous but vital: keeping the electrical systems of a manufacturing engineering laboratory working. The lab's machines built and tested space hardware, so breakdowns cost more than repair bills.

Neisler explains how the maintenance program grew as demands on it increased. Early on, the lab kept stocks of hard-to-get parts plus tubes, resistors, capacitors, and relays. As welding controls and machine tools grew more complex, that stock and the scrutiny of it had to grow too. The talk lays out the program for fellow engineers.
nasa-tm-19660030689-analysis-of-the-cali:
C. W. Murray Jr., of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this analysis in May 1966. Its subject is the calibration testing of the Varian R-20 rubidium frequency standards, highly precise timing devices built for the Apollo program. The tests themselves were run by the Bureau of Standards on three units from Varian Associates of Palo Alto, California.

Murray used least squares fits to describe how each standard's frequency drifted over time against the United States Frequency Standard. Daily readings strayed from their averages in a pattern matching a normal distribution fairly well. He also calculated each unit's drift over a full year. A straight-line fit, he found, predicted performance more steadily than higher-degree curves, staying within a tight tolerance for well over a year.
nasa-tm-19680006170-scale-model-study-of:
John F. Kline and Roy G. Stabe, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, studied swirling gas flow inside a rocket turbine manifold. The turbine drives the fuel pump of the M-1, a huge hydrogen-oxygen engine. Reference tests had shown puzzling pressure differences around its nozzle, blamed on the manifold.

The manifold is a ring-shaped pipe fed by one radial line. Kline and Stabe measured pressures around the ring on a scale model. They also took smoke trace photographs to see the flow. The pattern proved essentially symmetrical about the feedpipe. The pressure variation they mapped explains the nozzle exit patterns seen earlier.
nasa-tm-19680023437-off-design-theoretic:
Gerald A. Kraft and Brent A. Miller of Lewis Research Center calculate off-design performance for three turbofan engines in this 1968 memorandum. The geared-fan turbofans were sized for light subsonic aircraft. Off-design means running away from the exact conditions the engine was designed for.

The three engines came from preliminary exploratory studies, not a systematic parameter sweep. Still, they illustrate several ways to ease two classic problems. One problem is excessive turbine inlet temperature. The other is compressor surge, a dangerous breakdown of smooth airflow. The study used a bypass ratio and fan pressure ratio shared across the designs. Results show how each engine behaves across its operating range.
nasa-tm-19700005731-optimal-transfer-tra:
Rodney Bradford of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this technical memorandum in October 1969. It studies the best paths a spacecraft can take when it leaves an Earth parking orbit. Each path must end by meeting set conditions on the final orbit it reaches.

Bradford works out these transfer paths under several kinds of end conditions, called conic constraints. He also describes changes made to ROBOT, the computer program used for the work. Reports like this one helped planners pick sound flight paths and keep their design tools up to date.
nasa-tm-19700008419-sensing-molecular-we:
Milton J. LeRoy Jr. and Sol H. Gorland of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in January 1970. They tested a fluidic oscillator as a sensor for the molecular weight of gases. A fluidic oscillator has no moving parts and works by switching a jet of gas back and forth.

The team ran tests with simple and complex gases across a wide weight range. For steady flow, the switching rate matched the speed of sound in the gas. Simple gases and complex gases followed the same rule with different constants. The report also covers how pressure drop and temperature change the rate.
nasa-tm-19700026466-analysis-of-fm-degra:
How multipath effects degrade FM radio signals is analyzed in this Apollo internal note, number MSC-EE-R-68-16. It comes from the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston. Multipath means a signal reaches the receiver by several paths at once, after bouncing off nearby surfaces, and the copies can partly cancel each other.

The worry was an enclosed chamber like the orbital workshop, where walls sit close on every side. A communications team ran laboratory tests at the frequencies the workshop would use. Their results show spectrum distortion from multipath in the transmitted signal. A trial in a long enclosed tunnel copied workshop conditions, random objects and all, to see the effect at full scale.
nasa-tm-19700030523-cold-air-investigati:
Herman W. Prust Jr., Harold J. Schum, and Edward M. Szanca of the Lewis Research Center ran this turbine study. It is the first part of a cold-air investigation of transpiration-cooled stator blades. In this cooling scheme, air seeps out through the blade to shield it from hot gas.

This part reports the performance of a stator built with discrete holes for the cooling air. The team measured how the ejected coolant changed the stator's mass flow. They also measured its effect on efficiency. Cold-air rigs let engineers test turbine parts safely and cheaply. The results guide the design of cooled blades for real engines.
nasa-tm-19700032784-on-the-sharpness-of-:
John E. Srawley and E. Roberts Jr. of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper with J. L. Swedlow of Carnegie-Mellon University. It compares the sharpness of real cracks with Wells' crack opening displacement, called COD. The COD idea was widely used in British fracture research.

Wells' measure states how far the faces of a crack open under load. For mild overall bending, it ties simply to the force that grows the crack and to the metal's yield strength. The authors weigh this measure against an equivalent elastic crack. That model crack is longer than the real one but matches its near-tip stresses well.
nasa-tm-19710014504-cold-air-investigati:
NASA engineers reported part four of a cold air turbine study in April 1971, as NASA TM X-2176. The test turbine had stator blades cooled by transpiration. Coolant seeped out through a wire mesh shell on each blade. Hot turbine blades need such cooling to survive engine heat. Cold air tests let staff measure performance safely.

The single stage turbine ran across a range of speeds and pressure ratios. One set of runs held the coolant share near three percent of the main flow. Other runs varied coolant from zero to seven percent at design speed. Results were compared with other cooled designs. A plain uncooled turbine served as the yardstick.
nasa-tm-19710027948-implications-of-rego:
Verne R Oberbeck of the Ames Research Center wrote this October 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-62,089. It weighs what soil depth at the Apollo 16 landing site would mean for the mission. The lunar soil blanket is called regolith. It is built from the spray of countless small impacts. Apollo 11 and Apollo 12 had landed on basalt flows covered with such soil.

Oberbeck used a Monte Carlo impact cratering model to compute soil thickness. For many flat maria areas, its results matched estimates from small crater shapes. Apollo 16 would land in rougher highland terrain. Knowing the likely soil depth guided sampling plans and equipment choices. The paper extends a proven maria method to the new site.
navaho-houses-seventeenth-annual-report-:
Cosmos Mindeleff wrote Navaho Houses for the Bureau of American Ethnology at the Smithsonian. The piece ran in the bureau's seventeenth annual report, for 1895 to 1896. The Government Printing Office in Washington issued the report in 1898, under director J. W. Powell.

Mindeleff studies the homes of the Navaho people as a record of how they lived. Reports like this one filled the bureau's yearly volumes with field studies of native peoples. They paired text with plates and figures drawn from visits and notes. Modern readers use them as early, close records, while also noting the outlook of their time.
no-refuge-but-in-truth:
Goldwin Smith published No Refuge but in Truth at Toronto in 1908, with Wm. Tyrrell and Company. The Sun Printing and Publishing Company held copyright from 1907. Smith's preface says the letters collected here appeared in the New York Sun. He thanks that paper's editor for printing them.

Chapters treat man and his destiny, and new faith linked with old. The scope of evolution, and its limit, get two chapters. Explanations and the immortality of the soul follow. A last chapter asks if a revolution in ethics is coming. Smith, an old man of letters, defends plain truth against easy new creeds.
north-and-south:
Elizabeth Gaskell first published North and South in Household Words in 1854 and 1855, then in volume form in 1855. Her own note says the weekly form forced her to hurry events near the close. For the book she added short passages and several new chapters. She commends the tale, so mended, to the reader's kindness.

The record's summary names Margaret Hale, whose father leaves the Church on a point of conscience. The family moves from comfortable Hampshire to Milton, a northern mill town. Margaret first hates its ugliness, then sees the poverty of its workers. Chapter one, Haste to the Wedding, opens in Harley Street, with her cousin Edith asleep.
on-conducting-u-eber-das-dirigiren-a-tre: Richard Wagner wrote this treatise on conducting classical music. Edward Dannreuther translated it into English. The German title is Ueber das Dirigiren. The hosted sample preserves only the Project Gutenberg header. That header gives the title, author, and translator. It gives no readable text of the treatise itself. The header also notes the work treats style in performing classical music.
one-of-the-28th:
George Alfred Henty published this tale of Waterloo in 1890. A. L. Burt issued the illustrated New York edition. Henty's preface argues that a woman is the real heroine. A boy plays the principal part and faces adventures. Her nerve equals that of men in active warfare, he says.

Catalog notes name Herbert Penfold and young Ralph Conway. Penfold leaves his estate to a lost love's son. His jealous sisters plot to block that plan. Ralph joins the British Army against Napoleon Bonaparte. The 28th Regiment gives the tale its title. Henty praises women's courage in peril at length.
ordnance-instructions-for-the-united-sta: Ordnance Instructions for the United States Navy, in its fourth edition dated 1866, is the service's official manual for naval guns. The Navy Department's Bureau of Ordnance issued it just after the Civil War. The hosted sample shows the title pages and part headings only. Part One covers preparing vessels of war for battle. It also covers the duties of officers and men when at quarters. Part Two treats the equipment and maneuver of boats, and the exercise of boat howitzers. No instructional body text appears in the sample.
organic-syntheses-an-annual-publication-: Organic Syntheses, edited by James Bryant Conant, is an annual publication of laboratory procedures. Its subtitle promises satisfactory methods for the preparation of organic chemicals. The hosted sample contains only the Project Gutenberg front matter. That matter names the editor. It also warns that some numbers did not survive scanning correctly. Readers are told to check the 1941 print edition before attempting any procedure. No preparation text appears in the sample. This note therefore rests on the title and that editorial caution, and describes no individual synthesis.
phil-purcel-the-pig-driver-the-geography:
Phil Purcel, the Pig-Driver appears in Carleton's Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry, with The Geography of an Irish Oath and The Lianhan Shee beside it. Phil, Carleton says, was a singular character, for he never married, and a knave of the first water besides. Yet he was a general favourite.

The secret of his popularity was that he never laughed. His grave face made his feigned simplicity undetectable, and though he never smiled at his own gains, he made others laugh at their losses. Phil was also a miser, says Carleton, which best explains the gravity.
probabilities-an-aid-to-faith:
Martin Farquhar Tupper, known for his Proverbial Philosophy, argued the case for Christian belief in a book printed at Hartford by Silas Andrus and Son in 1851. His claim is that the main facts of the faith can be shown likely ahead of the proof drawn from records.

Tupper works by likeness, asking whether the state of the world would lead a thinker to expect such a faith to arise. He treats history, human nature, and the shape of events as signs that point one way. Readers get a calm, popular defence of religion in plain prose.
quotes-and-images-from-the-works-of-geor:
Quotes and Images from George Meredith is prepared by David Widger. It opens with pictures of the novelist. His sitting room at Flint Cottage is shown. Portraits at ages from thirty-five to eighty appear. Then come extracts from his works. They are set in alphabetical order.

A lover must have his delusions, the first lines say, just as a man must have a skin, and a madman gets madder when you talk reason to him. A dash of conventionalism makes the whole civilized world kin. A woman who goes beyond a string of pearls is in danger. Meredith's tragic comedian is named a grand pretender. He is a self-deceiver too.
recollections-of-my-childhood-and-youth:
George Brandes, the Danish critic known for a book on William Shakespeare, recalled his early years under four broad headings. The first, Discovering the World, moves from first impressions and school to the theatre and the King's Gardens. Boyhood's Years then fills in the family house, two grandfathers, teachers, and a mother at its heart.

Transitional Years treats schoolboy fancies, politics, and a religious crisis, with Hegel and Spinoza among his reading. Heine's Buch der Lieder had already fed his love of books in the boyhood chapters. Adolescence closes the set with the university prize contest, a meeting of Scandinavian students, and names such as Julius Lange and Björnstjerne Björnson.
recollections-of-my-youth:
Ernest Renan set down memories of his youth in a book whose contents page is dated 1897. The pieces are named for people and places of his early life. They include The Flax-Crusher, My Uncle Pierre, Good Master Système, and Little Noémi.

Two famed pieces stand in the list: Prayer on the Acropolis and a sketch called St. Renan. School days fill the last part, at the Petty Seminary of St. Nicholas du Chardonnet and then at the Issy Seminary. Each piece is short and told in parts. Renan looks back on the Breton world and the church schools that formed him.
report-on-the-condition-of-the-south:
Carl Schurz reported on the condition of the South in 1865, after touring states lately in rebellion. His report covers South Carolina, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and Louisiana. A report by Lieutenant General Grant on the same subject went with it, and both reached the Senate as an executive document of the 39th Congress.

The President's message of December 19, 1865, transmits them. It states that the rebellion has been suppressed and the United States holds every state where it existed. Courts, post offices, and revenue laws were being restored. The message adds that eight southern states had reorganized their governments, and all but Mississippi had ratified the amendment ending slavery.
rose-of-old-harpeth: Maria Thompson Daviess wrote Rose of Old Harpeth, issued in New York in 1911 with pictures by W. B. King. Daviess is named on the title page as the author of Miss Selina Lue, The Road to Providence, and The Melting of Molly. A picture captioned Rose Mary faces the title page. The author gives Rose Mary to her mother, Leonora Hamilton Daviess, and the whole book to her grandmother, who shared her own name, Maria Thompson Daviess.
ruth: Elizabeth Gaskell wrote Ruth, first issued in book form by Chapman and Hall in 1853. The contents list thirty-six chapters, opening with The Dressmaker's Apprentice at Work, Ruth Goes to the Shire-Hall, and Sunday at Mrs. Mason's. Later titles include Treading in Perilous Places, In North Wales, Troubles Gather About Ruth, and The Crisis. The middle chapters turn to Thurstan and Faith Benson, the dissenting minister's household, Ruth's first Sunday at Eccleston, Mother and Child, Leonard's christening, and Ruth as a governess in Mr.
schiller-wallenstein-coleridge-1800-deat:
Part 2 of Coleridge's Wallenstein, The Death of Wallenstein, appeared in 1800, completing his English version of Schiller's drama. Wallenstein, the imperial general in the Thirty Years' War, has dallied too long with treason. In this part the plots close in and the great man falls.

Astrology, omens, and old comrades' doubts surround Wallenstein as the Emperor's agents move against him. His daughter's love and his own pride hasten the end at Eger. Schiller built the fall as both history and tragedy of character. Coleridge's blank verse gave English readers the full force of it, and the translation stands among his best sustained works.
secret-band-of-brothers-a-full-and-true-:
Jonathan H. Green, who billed himself as a reformed gambler, wrote this expose of a hidden crime network said to span the United States. Green had already published books on gambling and his own life in that world. Engravings picture scenes from the account.

Green claims the band's members knew each other by secret signs and tokens in every part of the country. He lays out their crimes, tricks, and misdeeds as a warning to honest readers. The book mixes true-crime claims with moral alarm, and it shows how much fear of secret groups gripped American readers in Green's time.
select-speeches-of-kossuth:
Francis W. Newman cut and condensed these speeches by the Hungarian leader Kossuth, with Kossuth's own express leave. Newman warns that the full speeches sprawl like a tropical forest, strong but full of repeats. Heavy cutting, he argues, serves both present politics and lasting worth.

Newman's preface recalls the wild welcome Kossuth drew from crowds in lands not his own. He compares that fervor to the zeal that launched the First Crusade. Readers meet Kossuth as prophet and leader against crowned rulers, and they get his case for justice in a form shaped for the printed page.
senator-north:
Gertrude Atherton wrote this novel of Washington politics around a senator facing the hard school of the Senate. A long quoted warning fronts the book. It tells a new member how much he must learn and bear: censure he has not earned, sneers, and blame for aims he never held.

The quoted passage sets duty against the hunger for public praise. A senator must walk steadily in public duty, trusting time to do him justice. Atherton builds her tale on that strain between honor and ambition, giving readers a close view of power, party pressure, and private cost in the capital.
simo-n-boli-var-the-liberator-patriot-wa:
Guillermo A. Sherwell wrote this sketch of Simon Bolivar's life and work, first published at Washington in 1921. Sherwell (1878-1926) held doctorates from the National University of Mexico and from Georgetown, and served as rector in Mexico and as a legal adviser in Washington. A statue of the Liberator in New York fronts the book.

Bolivar stands here as patriot, warrior, statesman, and father of five nations. Sherwell had studied Spanish-American independence heroes for years and wrote a life of Sucre as well. Spanish versions of this life reached Bogota and Madrid, carrying Bolivar's fame in both directions.
strong-as-death:
Guy de Maupassant's novel Strong as Death opens in Part I with a chapter called A Duel of Hearts. Daylight pours through a skylight into a vast artist's studio, a severe room with high ceilings and draped walls, where the light softens among hangings and dies in the corners.

Unfinished portraits of great personages gleam in gilded frames, and the air holds paint, turpentine, and tobacco. Maupassant lingers on the weariness of the place after the master's daily struggle, as if the furniture itself had toiled with him. From this quiet studio the novel moves into a story of love, art, and aging in Paris society.
sydney-smith:
George W. E. Russell wrote Sydney Smith for the English Men of Letters series, printed at London in 1905. The book is a short life of the witty clergyman and Edinburgh Review writer whose table talk made him a legend of Regency and early Victorian London.

Russell explains his sources with unusual care. For nearly thirty years Lady Holland's memoir and Mrs. Austin's selection of letters formed the sole biography, prime in authority but lamentably inaccurate in dates. Lord Houghton's vivid monograph of 1873, Stuart Reid's sketch of 1884, and Leslie Stephen's dictionary article of 1898 added something, yet seemed to exhaust the record. Russell adds fresh material from Smith's descendants and from letters at Castle Howard and Holland House.
tanakh-jps-1917-ruth:
Ruth is a short story book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English Bible of the Jewish Publication Society. It is set in the days when the judges ruled, during a famine in the land of Judah.

Elimelech of Bethlehem takes his wife Naomi and their two sons to live in Moab to escape hunger. There he dies, the sons wed Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and in time both sons die too. Left alone, Naomi hears that God has given her people bread again and sets out for home. Readers follow Ruth's famed loyalty to her mother-in-law, a quiet tale of grief, gleaning, and fresh hope.
the-adventures-of-my-cousin-smooth: Timothy Templeton of Tewksbury wrote The Adventures of My Cousin Smooth, printed in New York and Auburn by Miller, Orton and Mulligan in 1856. Chapters listed send Mr. Smooth to Washington for a talk with General Cass, a dream, a hard path to the White House, and a dip into the dark corners of President Pierce's kitchen.
the-annual-monitor-for-1851-or-obituary-:
Number nine of a new series, The Annual Monitor for 1851 records the deaths of members of the Society of Friends in Great Britain and Ireland during 1850. London sellers C. Gilpin, R. Y. Clarke and Company, Darton and Company, and E. Marsh issued it in 1850, with George Hope at York.

An opening essay presents the year's count of the dead. The writers note that yearly totals usually run close, but this year shows a marked drop. They refuse to credit better health, calling the fall one of those swings that come and go across a run of years in a small body. The dead, they expect, will keep a steady share of the living over time.
the-book-of-the-bush-containing-many-tru: George Dunderdale wrote The Book of the Bush, put out in London by Ward, Lock and Company, with art by J. Macfarlane. The title page calls the tales true sketches. They deal with squatters, whalers, convicts, diggers, and others who left their home land. The list starts with Purging Out the Old Leaven and First Settlers. The wreck of the convict ship Neva on King's Island comes next. Then come the find of the River Hopkins, Whaling, Out West in 1849, and Among the Diggers in 1853.
the-boy-allies-in-great-peril-or-with-th:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies in Great Peril, or With the Italian Army in the Alps, dated 1916. The first chapter is called The Brewing Storm. It opens in Rome, where a vast crowd throngs the way to the king's palace. Chester, an American lad of some seventeen years, stops and grips his friend Hal by the arm.

Hal agrees the crowd is a sight, and Chester says a real army could be raised from it. Hal notes that most of them are soldiers in any case, since service is forced in Italy. The two trade views on the great question of the day. The Chamber of Deputies has fought to keep Italy out of the war, they say, but the voice of the folk must win in the end. Chester hopes Italy's ready army will tip the scales for the Allies.
the-boy-and-the-sunday-school-a-manual-o: John L. Alexander wrote The Boy and the Sunday School, a manual of principle and method for work with teen age boys. The Association Press of New York put it out in 1920, with rights dated 1913 from the International Committee of Young Men's Christian Associations. Marion Lawrance wrote the first word. Alexander gave the book to the superintendents of North America. Only the front pages and the start of the list are shown.
the-call-of-the-north:
Stewart Edward White wrote The Call of the North as a dramatized version of his own Conjurer's House, a romance of the free forest. White had also written The Westerners and The Blazed Trail. A verse at the front speaks of a land beyond the butternut, the maple, and the white pine, where shadows fall crimson across the snow. Chapter One sets a girl on a bank above a river flowing north.

At her back crouch a dozen clean whitewashed buildings. Before her, league on league into remoteness, stretches the stern northern wilderness, untrodden save by trappers, Indians, and beasts. Once a summer the sailing ship from England feels its frozen way through the Hudson Straits to the River of the Moose. In the brief summer the Indians come to trade their pelts, and the ship brings the goods she ordered a full year before.
the-canadian-brothers-or-the-prophecy-fu: The Canadian Brothers, by Major Richardson, is the first of two volumes. Its front matter carries an inscription to Sir John Harvey. It records the night of the 5th of June, 1813. That night 720 men of the 8th and 49th regiments routed 3,500 Americans at Stoney Creek. The Americans were under Generals Winder and Chandler, and both generals were taken prisoner. The preface is a letter from Windsor Castle dated October 29, 1832, about the presenting of a copy to His Majesty. No page of the tale is shown.
the-canadian-commonwealth: The Canadian Commonwealth, by Agnes C. Laut, was published by the Bobbs-Merrill Company at Indianapolis, with a copyright of 1915. Its opening pages give the contents: eighteen chapters and an index. The heads run on national consciousness and reciprocity rejected. They treat the coming of the English, the foreigner, and the Oriental. The Hindu, Panama, and the Hudson Bay route follow. Industrial problems, how Canada is governed, defense, and the domain of the North close the list. A heading for Chapter I follows, but no text of it is shown.
the-challenge-of-the-north:
James Hendryx wrote this northern adventure novel, published at Garden City, New York, by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1922. The tale opens in Terrace City, in the fur department of old John McNabb's big store. Oskar Hedin, who heads that department, studies a Russian sable coat spread on a table before him.

Hedin protests that the coat, priced at thirty thousand dollars, has no buyer in town, and a natural black fox piece at twenty thousand fares no better. Old John grins and points to Mrs. Orcutt, who did buy such a coat, though down in New York. Worse, she paid thirty-five thousand for a lighter, doctored piece. The exchange sets up a tale where fur wealth, pride, and northern trade drive the action, and where value is judged by sharp eyes.
the-cloister-and-the-hearth: Charles Reade wrote this novel, headed with the year 1861. Only the title page, a contents heading, and a bare list of chapter numbers are present here. An author's preface is named in the contents, but its text does not follow, and no chapter text is given. The plot therefore cannot be summed up from what is present.
the-collectors-being-cases-mostly-under-:
Frank Jewett Mather, Junr., published this story set in 1912 under a wry legal title: cases mostly under the ninth and tenth commandments. A ballade opens it, conceding the wrongfulness of art collecting. Seven stories follow, then reflections on art collecting that offer excuses for a practice usually judged pernicious.

The synopsis printed at the front names each case. Campbell Corot tells of an able and candid picture forger, and The del Puente Giorgione of an artful great lady and an artless expert. The Lombard Runes exposes duplicity in professional seekers for truth. Their Cross turns on an object of price that brought woe to a well-meaning New York couple. The Missing St Michael is called full of vanities and unfit for the simple reader, while The Balaklava Coronal shows a resourceful dealer triumphing over two critics and a captain of industry.
the-complete-poetical-works-of-oliver-go:
Austin Dobson edited Oliver Goldsmith's complete poetical works for this Oxford Edition, with an introduction and notes, and a portrait frontispiece after Sir Joshua Reynolds. His prefatory note is dated from Ealing in September 1906. The volume, he explains, is a reprint of the Selected Poems issued by the Clarendon Press in 1887, both extended and revised.

Extended means it now holds the whole of Goldsmith's poetry, not a selection. Revised means fresh annotation and illustration join the added text. Dobson says the bulk of the new editorial material was gathered at odd times over twenty years, and he warns that fresh Goldsmith facts are growing rare. He hopes he has acknowledged help wherever it was given. The contents promise an introduction, a chronology of Goldsmith's life and poems, then the descriptive poems, opening with The Traveller and The Deserted Village.
the-desire-of-the-moth:
Eugene Manlove Rhodes pairs two tales in The Desire of the Moth and the Come On, with illustrations by H. T. Dunn. The first tale opens in verse, a little song about a small girl next door. She loves the singer more than her elders do, marvels at his tales, and says they shall marry when she is grown.

The song stops short. John Wesley Pringle, at the mesa's last headland, draws rein and checks his ride, and the prose tale begins from that halt. The halt at the mesa's edge starts the tale proper.
the-dramatic-works-of-john-dryden-volume:
Volume one of The Dramatic Works of John Dryden pairs Sir Walter Scott's life of the poet with George Saintsbury's editing, in an 1882 Edinburgh printing. Saintsbury's preface calls Southey's Browne the best-edited book in English, and ranks Scott's Dryden near the top for scale, save for text work. He tells how he read it thrice: for pleasure, for lectures, and for a life sketch.

Scott's text is kept whole, its order and bulk untouched. Dryden's plays, from heroic drama to wit-driven comedy, fill the set. Scott frames the age as much as the man.
the-emigrant-mechanic-and-other-tales-in:
Thomas Cowherd's The Emigrant Mechanic and Other Tales in Verse joins verse tales with songs on Canadian themes. In his preface Cowherd owns his small schooling: born to a humble rank, put to a trade in his teens, and worked long hours for seven years. A short stay on a bush farm, he says, still taught him much of rural life worth telling.

His faith speaks out strong in the poems, drawn from close Bible study. Pieces first ran in local papers. Cowherd, a tinsmith poet of Brantford, sings of work, woods, and worship in plain, earnest rhyme.
the-excavations-of-roman-baths-at-bath:
On the Excavations of the Roman Baths at Bath, reprinted from volume eight of the Bristol and Gloucestershire Archaeological Society's Transactions, digs into old words as well as soil. It quotes Leland's visit of 1530, when he traced a sluice from the King's Bath to two priory baths and on to a mill above Bath bridge. Those lines, the paper says, had long puzzled scholars.

Spade work on the ground then tests the texts. Plans show the Roman baths as found. The paper helped fix how the great Roman bathing house at Aquae Sulis was laid out and fed.
the-five-books-of-youth:
Robert Hillyer wrote The Five Books of Youth as a set of poems first placed in journals such as The Nation, The Dial, and The New Republic. Five books divide the verse, from a mixed first book to days and seasons.

The first book holds pieces like Prothalamion, Montmartre, A Letter, Esther Dancing, and Thermopylae. The second turns to winds over a bay, gardens at dusk, and leaves on a green canal. Youth, love, war's shadow, and the turn of the year run through the set. Hillyer, author of Sonnets and Other Lyrics, writes in strict forms with a young man's grave music.
the-fortunate-youth:
William J. Locke wrote The Fortunate Youth as a novel of a boy raised in a grim north town and the luck that lifts him. Paul Kegworthy stands at the center from the first page.

Paul lives with his mother, her second husband Button, and six half-siblings in a grimy house in Bludston. Both parents work in a factory and take in lodgers. Button drinks, fights, and beats his wife; she in turn beats Paul, the one child not Button's own. No one knows who Kegworthy was, and a question on him earns the boy a frying pan on the head. From that hard start, chance opens a strange road up.
the-frost-spirit-and-other-poems-part-1-: John Greenleaf Whittier wrote the poems listed here under three heads: poems of nature, poems subjective and reminiscent, and religious poems, with The Frost Spirit first among them. Only the front matter and the full contents list are present here. The nature poems name Hampton Beach, a dream of summer, the lakeside, autumn thoughts, the mayflowers, and the trailing arbutus. No poem text follows in the pages given here, so the verse itself cannot be judged from the front pages alone.
the-girls-of-central-high-aiding-the-red:
Gertrude W. Morrison wrote The Girls of Central High Aiding the Red Cross. Its subtitle is Amateur Theatricals for a Worthy Cause. A contents list has twenty-five chapters. They run from The Oddest Thing That Ever Happened to It Is All Rounded Up. The heads name rehearsals, a mystery man, a bank-note, and an ice carnival. Chapter I opens in the glass-walled office of Laura Belding's father.

Laura sits at a high desk. From it she can look down on the office. She murmurs that the oddest thing has just happened. The heads promise schoolgirl actors raising funds for the Red Cross. They also promise a puzzle about a stranger. A missing boy named Purt adds to the puzzle. The tale blends stage fun and wartime aid work. It adds a light mystery for its young cast of Central High girls.
the-heart-s-highway-a-romance-of-virgini:
Mary E. Wilkins wrote The Heart's Highway, subtitled a romance of Virginia in the seventeenth century, published in New York in 1900. The narrator opens in 1682, at age thirty, riding one April Sabbath morning to meeting in Jamestown with Mistress Mary Cavendish, just turned eighteen. Slaves straggle behind them on the road.

Custom would have placed Mary's elder sister Catherine and her grandmother, Madam Judith Cavendish, on the ride as well. The grandmother, over seventy yet a strong rider, stays home at Drake Hill with rheumatism, and Catherine stays with her. The narrator notes Catherine's look of warning as Mary passed the door, and he insists her fear had no cause.
the-heart-s-secret-or-the-fortunes-of-a-:
Maturin Murray Ballou, writing as Lieutenant Murray, wrote The Heart's Secret; or, the Fortunes of a Soldier: a Story of Love and the Low Latitudes, published in Boston in 1852. A publisher's note says the novelette first ran in the Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion. The preface sets the story in Cuba, which Ballou calls a gem of the American archipelago.

Ballou praises the island's fields and shores and says a brief stay there gave him the matter for the tale. He claims care for facts of place and for the true belongings of the island. A second record in the library carries the same publisher's note and preface, stated here plainly so the shared front matter is clear.
the-hindu-yogi-science-of-breath: Yogi Ramacharaka wrote The Hindu-Yogi Science of Breath, described on its title page as a complete manual of the oriental breathing philosophy of physical, mental, psychic, and spiritual development. An index lists sixteen chapters, among them Breath Is Life, Nostril Breathing vs. Mouth Breathing, How to Acquire the Yogi Complete Breath, The Seven Yogi Developing Exercises, and Yogi Spiritual Breathing. Only the title page, index, and the first line of chapter one are present here, so the manual itself does not appear.
the-history-of-england-from-the-accessio:
T. F. Tout wrote The History of England from the Accession of Henry III to the Death of Edward III. The years covered are 1216 to 1377. Tout was a professor at the University of Manchester. His subject there was medieval and modern history. The volume forms one instalment of a larger work. That work is The Political History of England in twelve volumes.

A general preface for the series opens the book. It notes that seventy-six years had passed since Lingard finished his history. That history ended with the Revolution of 1688. Study had greatly advanced since then. Twelve writers would now set out the results of research. Each writer was chosen for his own period. The same series preface stands in a sibling volume.
the-history-of-england-from-the-norman-c: The Political History of England opens with a general preface. The same preface stands at the front of a sibling volume. It notes that seventy-five years had passed since Lingard finished his history. That history ended with the Revolution of 1688. The mass of materials had grown year by year since. Twelve writers would present the results of research in readable form. Each writer was chosen for his own period. Only the series preface is present here. The volume's own history text does not appear.
the-house-boat-boys-or-drifting-down-to-:
St. George Rathborne wrote The House Boat Boys, or Drifting Down to the Sunny South, also headed The House Boat Boys; or A Voyage to the Gulf. Rathborne is named as the author of Canoe Mates in Canada, Chums in Dixie, and The Young Fur Takers. Chapter one tells what a letter from a tramp steamer did.

At the post-office of a small town below Evansville, Indiana, rough Thad Tucker catches his friend Maurice Pemberton by the sleeve. Maurice has hard news he has half expected for four months. The old couple who gave him a home since his mother died are leaving for Chicago in a week. Their house is sold, turning him out with no place to sleep.
the-husbands-of-edith: George Barr McCutcheon wrote this novel, issued by Dodd, Mead and Company in New York in 1908 with illustrations by Harrison Fisher and decorations by Theodore B. Hapgood. The front matter lists his earlier successes, among them Graustark, Brewster's Millions, Beverly of Graustark, Nedra, and Jane Cable. Only the title pages and publisher's material are present here, so the story itself does not appear. A single illustration caption survives, in which a speaker begins a remark about Connie being perfect, hinting at the society comedy to come.
the-idea-of-progress-an-inquiry-into-its:
J. B. Bury wrote this inquiry into the idea of progress. He was Regius Professor of Modern History at Cambridge. He was also a Fellow of King's College. He dedicated the book to dead optimists. They include the Abbé de Saint-Pierre, Condorcet, and Auguste Comte. Herbert Spencer is also named. His preface argues a large point. Progress has become the ruling idea of western civilization. Belief or disbelief does not change that.

Bury shows the idea at work everywhere. Social theories must harmonize with it or fail. Liberty and democracy borrow strength from it. Socialism claimed it early. Even defenders of war call war its instrument. He contrasts that reign with the Middle Ages. The life beyond the grave then supplied the test. Institutions were judged by their harmony with that idea. The book traces how one guiding star replaced another.
the-interlude-of-wealth-and-health: The Malone Society issued this reprint of the early English interlude of Wealth and Health in 1907, printed at the Chiswick Press. Only the reprint's front matter and notes are present here. The play itself does not appear. The notes explain the black-letter original. Some letters have no modern match, so brackets carry their meanings. The long s has been changed to a short one. Speaker names are marked with plus signs. A note adds that the society's general editor prepared the reprint and Percy Simpson checked it.
the-island-of-faith: Margaret E. Sangster published this novel in 1921, dedicating it to M's M and Chance. Only the title page and contents are present here. The story itself does not appear. The contents open by introducing a settlement house. Quarrels and ideals follow. Rose-Marie comes to the rescue, and a lily in the slums appears. Bennie comes to the settlement house. An island, a decision, and Pa stepping aside come midway. Jim enters late. An answer, a miracle, and the happy ending close the list.
the-life-crime-and-capture-of-john-wilke:
George Alfred Townsend, a special correspondent, wrote his account of John Wilkes Booth and the Lincoln assassination conspiracy soon after the event. An explanatory note recalls his visit to Waterloo a year earlier. Files of newspapers from that battle day, kept in a museum there, struck him deeply.

Townsend argues that fresh news letters will serve future readers the same way for Lincoln death. His letters follow Booth crime, flight, and capture, plus pursuit, trial, and execution of the accomplices. Public feeling against assassination, North and South alike, frames a report written inside a consecrated time.
the-life-of-admiral-viscount-exmouth: Edward Osler wrote the life of Admiral Viscount Exmouth, and Routledge issued a new revised edition in London and New York in 1854. Only the title page, a dedication to the Navy, and the opening line of the preface are present here. That line begins a thought about wisdom at the start of hostilities whose scale nobody can foresee. The biography of the Pellew family admiral, hero of Algiers, remains outside this record.
the-life-of-george-washington-vol-1-comm: A five volume life of George Washington opens with this record, built from original papers bequeathed to Bushrod Washington. Only the title page is present here, and no author is named on it. The page says the work was compiled under Bushrod Washington inspection, with a prefixed introduction surveying English colonies in North America from settlement to the war for independence. The biography itself does not appear here.
the-life-of-george-washington-vol-2-comm: John Marshall wrote his life of George Washington from original papers left to Bushrod Washington, and this record holds volume two. Only the title page is present here, in wording that matches the other volume records in this set. It repeats the promise of a prefixed introduction on English colonies in North America up to the war for independence. The biography itself, covering Washington command and presidency in its full span, remains outside this record.
the-life-of-george-washington-vol-3-comm: John Marshall authorized life of George Washington appears here in a Sponsors Edition prepared for Henry H. Kimball. Only the front pages are present, naming Marshall as author and praising a Gilbert Stuart portrait of Washington valued at sixty thousand dollars. Stuart, the note says, thought Washington features showed strong, ungovernable passions held in check. The title page wording matches the other volume records in this set. The biography itself is missing from this record.
the-life-of-george-washington-vol-4-comm: John Marshall wrote his life of George Washington from original papers left to Bushrod Washington, and this record holds volume four. Only the title page is present here, in wording that matches the other volume records in this set. A prefixed survey of English colonies in North America, running from settlement to the independence war, is promised on that page. Readers looking for Washington later campaigns and his presidency will not find them in this record.
the-life-of-george-washington-vol-5-comm: Volume five closes the authorized life of George Washington that John Marshall compiled from family papers. Those papers came to Bushrod Washington as a bequest from his famous relative, and Marshall worked under Bushrod inspection. Only the title page is present here, with wording shared by the other volume records in this set. Its promised introduction surveys English colonies in North America before the war for independence. Washington last years, the ground of this closing volume, stay unseen here.
the-lion-of-the-north:
G. A. Henty addresses his preface to young readers and calls them dear lads, in a tale first published in 1886 according to the record heading. School years from twelve to eighteen, he argues, leave little time for foreign history. Yet the Thirty Years War shaped Europe deeply and deserves their study.

Emperor Ferdinand drive to crush Protestantism in Germany began that war, Henty says. German population fell by nearly a third across thirty years of fighting and suffering. His tale follows Sweden entry under Gustavus Adolphus, the Lion of the North, up to that king death in battle.
the-loom-of-youth:
Alec Waugh's The Loom of Youth was first published by Methuen in Great Britain in 1917 and reprinted many times within two years. The opening drops the reader into school talk at Fernhurst. Older boys dismiss Davenham, who is rotten at games and reads about fossils, and praise Meredith, who brought down Freeman in a match. Young Gordon, newly arrived, understands almost none of it.

What Gordon does grasp shocks him. Boys who wear the blue and gold ribbon seem exempt from the rules, and getting into the Fifteen forgives everything. His preparatory school taught that games only trained the body; at Fernhurst they are the one thing that matters. Waugh builds a school story around a new boy learning a hierarchy ruled by athletics.
the-lure-of-the-north: Harold Bindloss wrote The Lure of the North, published in New York by Frederick A. Stokes Company in 1918. Its title page notes it appeared in England as Agatha's Fortune. Only the title page and a list of Bindloss's other books are present here, so the novel does not appear. That list runs to nearly thirty titles. Among them are Alton of Somasco, Prescott of Saskatchewan, Winston of the Prairie, The Gold Trail, and Delilah of the Snows. They mark Bindloss as a prolific writer of northern and prairie fiction.
the-magnetic-north: Elizabeth Robins, writing as C. E. Raimond, published The Magnetic North in 1904, with a map. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the novel does not appear. The seventeen chapter titles place the story in the Yukon: Winter Camp in the Yukon, House-Warming, The Blow-Out, The Shaman, A Penitential Journey, Kaviak's Crime, and Christmas. Princess Muckluck, Holy Cross, The Great White Silence, The Pit, and The Great Stampede follow. Robins's other books named on the title page include The Open Question and Below the Salt.
the-man-in-gray-a-romance-of-north-and-s:
Thomas Dixon subtitled The Man in Gray a romance of North and South. He dedicated it to his fellow members of the Kappa Alpha fraternity. The fraternity was founded, he notes, under the inspiration of Robert E. Lee in 1868. A note to the reader makes an unusual claim: Dixon calls the book the strangest fiction he ever wrote because, he insists, it is true. Every character is historic, he says, he has not changed even a name, and he holds proofs for each event.

A list of leading characters is headed by Robert E. Lee, the Southern commander, with his wife, his older son Custis, his daughter Mary, and his sister Mrs. Marshall. Household figures follow, including Uncle Ben the butler and Sam, listed as a slave. Whatever a reader makes of Dixon's claim, the book presents itself as history retold as romance, centered on Lee's family.
the-man-who-rocked-the-earth: Arthur Train and Robert Williams Wood wrote The Man Who Rocked the Earth, copyrighted in 1915 by Doubleday, Page and Company. Only the reprint front matter of a 1974 Arno Press edition and an epigraph are present here, so the novel itself does not appear. The epigraph, from W. L. Comfort in November 1914, dwells on the delicacy of the world's position. Human life depends on the small matter of the tilt of the poles. Men are products of earth's precarious position and her still more precarious tilt.
the-masque-of-the-red-death:
Edgar Allan Poe's short story The Masque of the Red Death opens on a country emptied by a hideous plague. The disease marks its victims with scarlet stains and kills within half an hour. Prince Prospero answers by gathering a thousand healthy friends into a walled abbey. The courtiers weld the iron gates shut and settle inside with provisions, musicians, dancers, and wine.

After five or six months of seclusion, Prospero stages a masked ball of unusual magnificence. Poe describes the seven rooms of the imperial suite, each dressed in a single color, from blue at the eastern end to purple next. Stained-glass windows match the hue of every chamber, and sharp turns break the view from room to room. Readers watch pleasure and pride seal themselves in against a death that respects no wall.
the-meaning-of-truth:
William James published The Meaning of Truth as a sequel to his book Pragmatism. The preface restates the part of that earlier work he calls pivotal: the account of truth as a relation between an idea and its object. Pragmatists and intellectualists alike, James says, accept that truth means agreement with reality. The dispute concerns what agreement actually amounts to when ideas do not copy their objects.

James answers with his famous cash-value question: what concrete difference does a belief's truth make in actual life? True ideas, he argues, are those we can assimilate, validate, corroborate, and verify. Truth is not a stagnant property inside an idea; it happens to an idea through events. An idea becomes true by verifying itself in experience. Readers get James defending pragmatism's theory of truth in his own most careful terms.
the-notorious-mrs-ebbsmith:
Arthur Wing Pinero wrote the play The Notorious Mrs. Ebbsmith, set in Venice at Easter time. The cast lists Agnes, Lucas Cleeve and his wife Sybil, Sir Sandford Cleeve, the Duke of St. Olpherts, and the Rev. Amos Winterfield, among others. A week passes between the first and second acts.

The first act opens in a fine but faded room in the Palazzo Arconati, a lodging house on the Grand Canal. Two Venetian servants, Antonio Poppi and Nella, clear the breakfast table in the sun. Pinero mixes grand rooms with cheap, showy furnishings, a visual hint of lives that look finer than they are.
the-outdoor-girls-in-florida-or-winterin: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls in Florida, or Wintering in the Sunny South, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists show Florida as the fifth Outdoor Girls volume, after Deepdale, Rainbow Lake, a Motor Car, and a Winter Camp, priced at 40 cents postpaid. Hope's Bobbsey Twins books for little men and women follow.
the-rangers-or-the-tory-s-daughter-a-tal:
D. P. Thompson, author of The Green Mountain Boys, returns to Vermont's Revolutionary history in a tenth edition issued in two volumes bound as one. His preface explains that Bennington and the northern campaign of 1777 were held back from the earlier book to keep its unity.

Ten years later he offers the deferred material as a separate tale, warning that history matters more to him here than mere story. The first chapter opens with verse about a mountain home. Readers who like early American historical fiction will find a deliberate blend of documented events and invented lives.
the-record-of-a-quaker-conscience-cyrus-: Cyrus Pringle's diary is presented by Macmillan at New York in 1918, with an introduction by Rufus M. Jones and earlier copyright held by the Atlantic Monthly Company in 1913. Here only the publisher's imprint pages and title pages for the diary are present, so the diary entries themselves do not appear at all.
the-ruins-or-meditation-on-the-revolutio:
C. F. Volney's The Ruins, or Meditation on the Revolutions of Empires, is joined here with The Law of Nature in a New York edition from the Twentieth Century Publishing Company dated 1890. The volume also adds Volney's answer to Dr. Priestly, a biographical notice by Count Daru, and material on the zodiacal signs and constellations by the editor.

The publisher's preface explains that recently purchased stereotype plates proved so worn by many editions that resetting the whole work in modern type was decided instead. That choice let the publisher restore the translator's preface from the original edition and recover notes and other valuable material carelessly omitted from the American reprint.
the-story-of-my-boyhood-and-youth: John Muir's memoir of his boyhood and youth came out in March 1913. Houghton Mifflin published it. His own sketches illustrate it. The impression followed Atlantic Monthly copyrights of 1912 and 1913. Only the title pages and the start of a contents list are present here. The list opens with a boyhood in Scotland. Its heads name earliest recollections, school fights, and birds'-nesting. A new world and stories of America follow. Muir's narrative itself does not appear.
the-story-of-the-mormons-from-the-date-o:
William Alexander Linn wrote this secular history of the Mormons from their origin to 1901, and his preface calls their story the American chapter longest left unwritten. Church histories are hopelessly biased, Linn says. Trustworthy works cover only certain periods. Exposures by former members rest under suspicion. Personal bias may taint them. Most people know only two things: polygamy and Brigham Young.

Linn aims at a connected history. It rests largely on Mormon sources. Mother Smith's picture of the early church is one. Joseph Smith's own account is another. It covers the golden plates and his doings almost day by day. Accounts by Parley P. Pratt and Lorenzo Snow follow. Church periodicals from Ohio, Missouri, Illinois, and England complete the sources. He argues that Sidney Rigdon, known to few even by name, was the real originator of the scheme for a new church.
the-story-of-the-treasure-seekers-being-:
E. Nesbit opens the Bastable children's hunt for a fortune. She dedicates the book to Oswald Barron. Without him, she says, it could never have been written. A contents list promises lively episodes. A council of ways and means leads off. Digging for treasure follows. Detectives, bandits, and editors appear. A poet and a divining-rod close the list. The narrator begins with an insistence. The children were not lazy about the looking.

The narrator, who soon emerges as Oswald, first sets the scene properly: the ancestral home is a semi-detached house in the Lewisham Road with a small garden. There are six Bastables besides Father, their mother is dead, and Dora is eldest, followed by Oswald, Dicky, the twins Alice and Noel, and Horace Octavius, the youngest.
the-tragedy-of-macbeth: Shakespeare's Tragedy of Macbeth is the work named here, yet the pages present repeat the general editor's note by Michael S. Hart found at the front of several plays in this set. The note explains old printers' letter exchanges, type packed into cliches, and why apparent errors are left uncorrected as canonical. Hart even illustrates the point with the first lines of Hamlet, not Macbeth. No witches and no line of the Scottish play appears in what is shown, so the record documents an edition's preface, not the tragedy.
the-truth-about-jesus-is-he-a-myth: M. M. Mangasarian's Truth About Jesus asks on its title page, Is He a Myth?, under Huxley's question about what becomes of Christianity if the Gospel events are not historically true. This record gives the illustrated front matter and a full contents list. Parts move from the problem stated, through the Christian documents, virgin births, the origin of the cross, and the silence of contemporary writers, to modern opinions of Jesus. An appendix answers clerical critics. Mangasarian's freethought argument is mapped here, its chapters beginning past these leaves.
the-underground-city-or-the-black-indies:
Jules Verne sets The Underground City in the Aberfoyle coal mines of Scotland. The copy here comes from volume nine of his works, edited by Charles F. Horne and published in New York in 1911. The story also carries the names The Black Indies and The Child of the Cavern.

Chapter one begins with a mysterious letter summoning engineer James Starr to the Dochart pit the next day. Harry Ford, son of old overman Simon Ford, will wait at Callander station to meet him. Promised a communication of an interesting nature, Starr heads toward a worked-out mine. Chapter titles ahead promise strange phenomena, an experiment, a settlement called Coal Town, and a girl named Nell.
the-visits-of-elizabeth:
Elinor Glyn's Visits of Elizabeth had reached a twenty-second edition by 1901, issued at Cambridge in the United States. Elizabeth, about seventeen, begins paying visits among her well-connected kin after a childhood spent largely abroad with an invalid mother. Ancestors reaching back to the Conquest, plus two countesses and a duchess among her relatives, smooth her way.

Her first letter home comes from Nazeby Hall during Cricket Week, dated July 26. Contents pages map a social tour: Eaton Place, Heaviland Manor, Hazeldene Court, a château at Croixmare visited repeatedly, a yacht, Havre, Retby, Carriston Towers, and Chevenix Castle. The form is a girl's candid letters reporting the great houses she tours, one visit at a time.
the-winning-of-barbara-worth:
Harold Bell Wright's Winning of Barbara Worth opens with an acknowledgment dated at Tecolote Rancho on April 25, 1911. The story, he insists, is not a history of the Colorado Desert's transformation into the Imperial Valley, nor any person's biography. Still, that reclamation work, turning a desolate waste into homes, cities, and farms within ten years, was his inspiration.

Wright thanks engineers and surveyors of the reclamation by name, including men of the California Development Company and William Mulholland of the Los Angeles Aqueduct. The book is inscribed to W. F. Holt for his life and work in the valley. Contents chapters begin with Into the Infinite Long Ago, Jefferson Worth's offering, and Miss Barbara Worth herself.
the-world-english-bible-web-ruth:
Ruth, book eight in the World English Bible, unfolds during the judges' era. Famine drives Elimelech from Bethlehem to Moab. His wife Naomi and sons Mahlon and Chilion go along. Elimelech dies there, leaving Naomi with the boys. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. About ten years pass in that foreign country.

Then both sons die as well. Naomi is left without husband or children. She resolves to return home to Judah. One daughter-in-law will refuse to leave her side. Loyalty between women drives this quiet story. A small family's survival leads, eventually, to King David's ancestry.
the-world-s-great-sermons-volume-02-hook:
Volume two of The World's Great Sermons, compiled by Grenville Kleiser, opens with a biographical note on Thomas Hooker, a Cambridge graduate and fellow born in 1586. He took a small Surrey parish in 1620. His reformed preaching drew notice by 1629. Bishop Laud's threats drove him first to Holland. In 1633 he sailed with John Cotton for New England.

Hooker settled at Newtown, now Cambridge, Massachusetts. Kleiser calls him practically a founder of Connecticut. The sermon that follows treats Abraham's imitators and active faith. Each preacher in the set gets such a life sketch. Readers can trace English and American preaching across centuries in these volumes.
the-young-mother-management-of-children-: William A. Alcott's The Young Mother, dated 1836, is shown through an advertisement for its enlarged third edition and a detailed contents list. Alcott added a section on managing the mother herself. Chapter one treats the nursery, its walls, windows, and furniture. Chapter two covers temperature and keeping infants warm. The advice itself begins beyond the pages present in this record, so only the book's plan can be described from them.
the-young-voyageurs-boy-hunters-in-the-n:
Captain Mayne Reid, in The Young Voyageurs, invites his boy reader north in chapter one. He asks whether the boy has heard of the Hudson's Bay Company.
