Furs in a muff, boa, or dress trimming likely came through it. Reid offers to explain the country those furs come from. The animals behind them also deserve attention, he says. He proposes crossing the fur countries from south to north together.

The journey will cover many thousand miles, he warns. No railway, steamboat, stage-coach, or even horse will help. No hotels or roadside inns await the travelers. Boy hunters must live off a vast northern wilderness instead. Reid's direct address made generations of boys feel personally recruited for adventure.
the-yukon-trail-a-tale-of-the-north: William MacLeod Raine's The Yukon Trail, copyrighted in 1917, is shown here through its title pages alone. Grosset and Dunlap published the tale of the north in New York. George Ellis Wolfe supplied the illustrations. One caption describes a man catching a woman by the shoulders. Raine also wrote Wyoming and Bucky O'Connor. The story chapters themselves do not appear in the pages present in this record.
tom-swift-and-his-wireless-message-or-th: Victor Appleton's series is listed at length in this record, with subtitles for each early Tom Swift book. The list runs from the motor-cycle, motor-boat, airship, and submarine boat through the electric runabout to this volume, the castaways of Earthquake Island. No contents or chapter from the wireless message story itself appears after the list. Readers can trace the young inventor's machines in order from these pages, while Appleton's island adventure itself is not shown in this record.
town-and-country-or-life-at-home-and-abr: John S. Adams published Town and Country, or Life at Home and Abroad, Within and Without Us, at Boston in 1855. A contents list mixes stories, songs, and poems. Saved by Kindness, The Love of Elinore, and Tis Sweet to Be Remembered open the collection. Later titles include Voices from the Spirit Land, Mount Vernon and Washington's tomb, Freedom's Gathering, a wine-dealer's clerk, and letters on letter-writing. Love That Wanes Not closes the list. A contents list alone is on these pages, so Adams's pieces themselves are not shown.
travels-in-england-during-the-reign-of-q:
Paul Hentzner, a German lawyer born at Crossen in 1558, toured England late in Queen Elizabeth's reign. The 1892 Cassell edition prints his account beside Sir Robert Naunton's Fragmenta Regalia, observations on Elizabeth's court and favourites. An introduction sketches both men and the England they describe.

Hentzner became tutor to a young Silesian nobleman in 1596 and travelled with him for three years. Their route crossed Switzerland, France, England, and Italy. Back in Germany, he published his Latin account at Nuremberg in 1612. Readers get an outsider's close look at Elizabeth, London, and the great men of the court.
trials-and-triumphs-of-faith:
Mary Cole's Trials and Triumphs of Faith opens with a preface that argues for a church history written through lives. World history, it says, records human deeds, from Washington and Joan of Arc to Nero. Church history instead records God's work through willing instruments, often the weak rather than the mighty.

The preface then introduces Sister Mary Cole herself. Pain racked her body from childhood, and ill health denied her schooling. Such a start seemed to shut her out of any useful place. Friends who had been helped by her faith pressed her to write, and the book tells how God healed her and fitted her for service.
uppingham-by-the-sea-a-narrative-of-the-:
Uppingham by the Sea tells how Uppingham School spent a year at Borth, on the Welsh coast. Macmillan issued the book at London in 1878, and the author signs only initials, J. H. S. A Latin dedication honors Edward Thring, the school's head, and the assistant masters who stood by the boys when the school's safety hung in doubt.

The preface explains the book's roots. In the spring of 1876 and of 1877, letters under the same title ran in The Times and drew the interest of the school's friends. Those sketches lent their name to this fuller narrative of the same events. The writer claims one clear fitness for the task: direct knowledge of what happened. Readers get a detailed record of a famous episode, when a great school picked itself up and carried on by the sea.
virgilia-or-out-of-the-lion-s-mouth:
Felicia Buttz Clark wrote Virgilia, or Out of the Lion's Mouth, in 1917, a tale of early Christian Rome. Her contents promise a confession of faith, a little fish, the hymn of the water-carrier, the inner shrine of Jupiter, a feast of grapes, and the entrance of Lycias the gladiator. Chapter one opens in the Circus at Rome on a day in June, about two thousand years ago.

A crowd of one hundred thousand fills the white marble tiers under the open sky, watching a gladiator fight in the arena below. At the western end stands the emperor's box, flanked with tall Corinthian pillars and hung with the arms of the Roman people. In it sits one of the cruelest emperors Rome ever suffered under, his purple cloak thrown carelessly back in the heat. Clark sets her Christian heroine's trial in that arena's shadow, where faith faced the lions.
visit-to-iceland-and-the-scandinavian-no:
Madame Ida Pfeiffer's Visit to Iceland and the Scandinavian North appeared in English in a second edition in 1853. Ingram, Cooke, and Company issued it at London. The rendering came from her German, with many notes and eight tinted engravings. A note to the first edition says the success of her Woman's Journey round the World, in the same series, prompted this volume. Iceland was then little known and little written of.

The editor added notes wherever the text seemed to need them. The volume adds more than Pfeiffer. It holds an essay on Icelandic poetry by M. Bergmann, and a rendering of the old Icelandic poem the Voluspa. A brief sketch of Icelandic history follows. A version of Schiller's ballad The Diver, which Pfeiffer cites, closes the additions. Readers get a woman traveller's Iceland with a small library of northern lore bound in.
wandering-heath: Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch published Wandering Heath in 1895, a book of tales from his Cornwall. A note at the front lists where each story first ran. The Roll-Call of the Reef ran in The Idler. The Looe Die-hards ran in The Illustrated London News. Others ran in The Pall Mall Magazine, The Strand, and The Speaker. Pages present here hold that note and the contents only. Titles promise a prologue, wrestlers, and the Bishop of Eucalyptus.
war-poetry-of-the-south:
William Gilmore Simms edited War Poetry of the South. Richardson and Company entered it for copyright in 1866, at New York. He inscribed the volume to the women of the South. They have lost a cause, he writes, but they have made a triumph. They proved themselves worthy of the best womanhood. They taught noble lessons of effort and endurance to their children.

His preface gives the book's reasons. The poems form a gift to the nation's literature, he argues. They show the growth of mind and art in a large section of the country, under conditions sure to stir talent and provoke expression. The volume is sectional in character, he grants. It bears a temper born of the war years. Readers get the verse the South wrote about its own war, gathered by its leading man of letters while the wounds were fresh.
westcott-kabir-panth:
G. H. Westcott published Kabir and the Kabir Panth in 1907. His study gives the classic English account of the weaver-saint. Kabir's sect, the Panth that bears his name, fills the second half.

Kabir's verses lash priestcraft in both Hindu and Muslim camps alike. He mocks empty rite and praises the God found in the heart. Westcott traces the saint's life, songs, and the order that spread them. His book rests on texts and talks with Kabir's own followers. Readers meet India's most quoted mystic in a clear, warm, firm guide. Westcott's respect for Kabir's bite keeps the study fresh today.
wild-wings-a-romance-of-youth: Nothing beyond the title page and contents is present here for Margaret Rebecca Piper's Wild Wings, a romance of youth from 1921, so her tale does not appear. The contents open with a chapter called Mostly Tony. Tony meets Rosalind, dances into a discovery, and faces bitter fruit in the listed chapters. Other titles name a girl who could not stop being a princess and a boy who behaved like an ass. A wedding ring hard to remember and a young man not for sale close the list.
wordsworth: F. W. H. Myers wrote this life of the poet William Wordsworth. Pages present here hold a contents list covering twelve chapters, but no chapter text. The chapters trace Wordsworth from birth and Cambridge through London and France. Later chapters cover the Lyrical Ballads, Grasmere, marriage, and Rydal Mount. Final chapters treat poetic diction, natural religion, an Italian tour, and the laureateship. The life itself does not begin in these pages.
youth:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this autobiographical novel, rendered into English by C. J. Hogarth. The narrator dates his youth from a friendship with Dimitri. That friendship taught him that man's destiny is moral improvement, which felt easy and lasting in theory. In practice his life stayed petty, muddled, and pleasure-seeking. Virtuous thoughts pleased his mind yet left his feelings untouched, he admits.

A sudden moment of fresh moral force changed him at nearly sixteen. Tutors and a supervisor still ran his days as university neared. He fretted over his plain face in mirrors. Readers get a frank record of a young conscience waking up.
